One Spectrum, Two Resources:
Data–Memory Scaling in Autoregressive Prediction

Chiwun Yang ††thanks: christiannyang37@gmail.com. City University of Hong Kong.    Xiaoyu Li ††thanks: xiaoyu.li2@unsw.edu.au. University of New South Wales.
Abstract

How much learned memory is needed to benefit from more data? We show that the two resources are governed by one predictive-energy spectrum in a positive-entropy autoregressive retrieval source. Each coordinate contributes its query probability times the squared radius of its unknown logit. Writing μ\mu for the resulting energy spectrum, we prove the minimax law ℜvalue∗(n,B)≍RΦμ(n−1)+Φμ(τB),Φμ(t)=∫min{x,t}μ(dx),\mathfrak{R}^{*}_{\rm value}(n,B)\asymp_{R}\Phi_{\mu}(n^{-1})+\Phi_{\mu}(\tau_{B}),\Phi_{\mu}(t)=\int\min\{x,t\}\,\mu(\mathrm{d}x), for nn prediction blocks and a learned state with at most 2B2^{B} values. Data set the resolution 1/n1/n; memory sets the level τB\tau_{B} reached by optimal bit allocation. The complete curve also recovers the positive spectrum. Energy–dimension pairing is essential: two causal sources with identical block-energy and block-dimension marginals have different data and memory exponents. A masked query–key attention head learns the route and values, realizing the law with explicit routing, format, and arithmetic errors. Further results give exponent-adaptive allocation, finite-precision realization, and compute–precision laws under two-sided arithmetic assumptions. Experiments recover the data–memory collapse and coupling exponents, explain the routing and allocation mechanisms, and examine weight-only quantization across six pretrained-model scales.

1 Introduction

More data reveal more predictive structure, but a predictor benefits only from what its learned state can retain. When should we collect more data, and when should we increase learned memory? Empirical scaling laws relate loss to data, model size, and compute (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). To understand how these resources work together, we seek a property of the prediction problem that determines both the information available in finite data and the information preserved by a finite learned state.

Consider a prediction task with many independently varying pieces of knowledge. A piece that is queried often or strongly changes the next-token probability deserves more learning and storage resources than one that is rarely used or has little predictive effect. Our model expresses each piece as an unknown scalar prediction parameter, called a coordinate. The key quantity is predictive energy per independent coordinate. In our autoregressive source, coordinate ii has query probability pip_{i} and an unknown logit, or log-odds of a binary target, in [−Ri,Ri][-R_{i},R_{i}]. Its predictive energy qi=pi​Ri2q_{i}=p_{i}R_{i}^{2} measures its potential contribution to prediction error. Collecting these energies, counting repeated values separately, gives the spectrum. At a chosen error resolution, small coordinates contribute their whole energy and larger coordinates contribute only the unresolved portion. Adding these contributions defines a spectral curve. Finite data and finite learned memory read the same spectral curve at different resolutions.

This connection gives a joint resource law. Let nn count independent training blocks and let BB count the bits retained after training, so the learner can finish in at most 2B2^{B} different states. We measure excess cross-entropy above the loss of a predictor that knows the true conditional probabilities. First consider value estimation with the relevant coordinate revealed. Data set an error resolution of order 1/n1/n; memory allocates bits until retained coordinates reach a common residual-error level. The smallest worst-case expected excess loss is, up to constants, the sum of the spectral curve at these two resolutions. This minimax result allows unrestricted training computation and joint coding across coordinates. Section 3 defines the source, risk, and two resolutions before stating the full formula.

The law makes the resource balance explicit. List coordinate energies in decreasing order and suppose q(i)≍i−(1+χ)q_{(i)}\asymp i^{-(1+\chi)}, where χ>0\chi>0 is their decay exponent and ≍\asymp denotes equality up to constant factors. The two terms scale as n−χ/(1+χ)+B−χn^{-\chi/(1+\chi)}+B^{-\chi} and balance at B≍n1/(1+χ)B\asymp n^{1/(1+\chi)}. Below this memory scale, retaining learned information is the bottleneck; above it, observations matter more. More generally, an energy group can spread its total energy across several independent coordinates. Increasing that dimension produces more parameters to learn, each with less predictive energy. The general scaling corollary quantifies this effect through the distribution of coordinate energies. The full spectral curve applies beyond power laws and recovers every positive coordinate energy with its multiplicity.

This perspective reveals information that separate scaling descriptors discard. Concentrating energy in one coordinate makes it easier to learn and retain than spreading it across many independent coordinates. We construct two causal sources with exactly the same block-energy and block-dimension multisets at every dyadic level. Pairing high energy with small blocks or large blocks changes the coordinate spectrum and both resource exponents. The pairing, not either marginal alone, determines how predictive information is distributed.

The source also makes the learning mechanism explicit. Each regeneration block contains KK candidate tokens, a query, and a stochastic next token. An unknown route selects the relevant candidate, whose bounded Bernoulli logit is also unknown. Calibration blocks reveal the correct candidate; prediction blocks teach its value; evaluation uses independent held-out blocks. Fixed embeddings and projections contain neither unknown object. A fixed-key, trainable-query attention head learns the route, followed by frequency-preconditioned output-parameter learning. Its masked query–key scores and gradients match the construction in the proof, connecting the spectral law to a concrete two-stage learner.

The same resource picture organizes representation and computation. A universal allocation schedule adapts to an unknown power-law exponent when coordinate order is known. Finite-precision evaluation quantifies routing, storage, and arithmetic errors. For the specified dense computational graph, operation counts and numerical assumptions connect the precision needed for a target error to bit complexity and conditional compute phases. These results explain how statistical resolution becomes a representational and computational requirement.

  • •

    One spectrum, two resources. An exact truncated-energy curve expresses both terms of arbitrary-state minimax risk, recovers the positive spectrum, and determines the data and learned-memory exponents. A masked-attention learner realizes the spectral surface with explicit routing, format, and arithmetic errors; adaptive allocation and precision analysis connect this law to implementation.

  • •

    Why separate marginals fail. Same-marginal causal sources have different coordinate spectra and different data and memory exponents. Their energy–dimension pairing identifies the information missing from separate scaling descriptors.

Our experiments vary sample and state budgets on a fixed source, test same-marginal separation, and compare learned, known, and frozen routing. Interventions and perturbed energy profiles examine the mechanisms behind the measured curves. Continued training tests the interaction between added data and deployed storage, while weight-only post-training quantization across six pretrained Transformer scales measures the effect of numerical representation at fixed checkpoints.

2 Related Work

Our question connects scaling laws, finite-rate representation, and distribution-specific learning: which source statistic determines the value of additional observations and additional learned memory? The following literatures provide the statistical and computational ingredients. Table 1 summarizes the closest theorem-level connections.

Empirical and mechanistic scaling laws.

Empirical studies found extended power-law regimes in neural prediction as data, model size, and computation grow (Hestness et al., 2017; Kaplan et al., 2020; Henighan et al., 2020). Compute-optimal work asks how a training budget should be divided between parameters and tokens (Hoffmann et al., 2022), while routed models distinguish total parameters from parameters used per token (Clark et al., 2022). Extrapolation studies, broken-power-law fits, and replications show that fitted exponents depend on the model family, resource definition, and training prescription (Alabdulmohsin et al., 2022; Caballero et al., 2023; Porian et al., 2024). Theoretical accounts derive learning curves from task dimension, spectral decay, or simplified dynamics (Sharma and Kaplan, 2020; Bordelon et al., 2020; Bahri et al., 2024); solvable random-feature and dynamical models separate data-, width-, and time-limited phases (Maloney et al., 2022; Bordelon et al., 2024; Paquette et al., 2024). A discrete-skill model obtains aggregate power laws from decreasing skill frequencies (Michaud et al., 2023). Knowledge-capacity studies instead translate factual prediction loss into retained information and estimate bits per parameter (Allen-Zhu and Li, 2025; Morris et al., 2025). A compression model with frequency-ranked knowledge derives both data and model scaling laws (Pan et al., 2025), while an optimization analysis of multilayer Transformers derives resource-dependent generalization phases (Yang, 2025). We connect the data and learned-memory axes through a common source spectrum. Its tail determines both rates, and its construction identifies the energy–dimension pairing on which those rates depend.

Finite-rate estimation and memory.

Rate–distortion theory characterizes the smallest coding rate compatible with a prescribed distortion, and classical quantization theory develops the geometry of finite codebooks (Shannon, 1959; Gray and Neuhoff, 1998). Quantized Gaussian sequence estimation gives sharp arbitrary-codebook storage–risk trade-offs, smoothness adaptation over Sobolev classes, and multiple data–communication regimes (Zhu and Lafferty, 2014; Zhu and Lafferty, 2018b; Zhu and Lafferty, 2018a). Related theories bound working memory, sequential estimator states, retained sample information, or Bayesian minimum excess risk (Steinhardt and Duchi, 2015; Berg et al., 2021; Feldman et al., 2025; Hafez-Kolahi et al., 2021). Writing BB for retained bits, we constrain the final learned state to at most 2B2^{B} values while allowing unrestricted training computation. Functional quantization is especially close to our spectrum calculation: regularly varying covariance eigenvalues determine sharp Hilbert-space quantization rates, and product quantizers attain them (Luschgy and Pagès, 2004; Luschgy et al., 2010). Our additional step is a uniform finite-resource risk bound for random coordinate observations: each observation queries one unknown binary prediction parameter, and all logits vary independently within bounded intervals. It accounts for coordinates with few or no visits while allowing any final 2B2^{B}-state encoder. The same curve then expresses sample and retained-state error. The same-marginal construction resolves an identification question: separate block-energy and block-dimension distributions do not determine the coordinate spectrum.

Neural quantization and precision.

Mixed-precision training retains high precision where it is numerically useful (Micikevicius et al., 2018). Mean-field, Hessian-aware, and learned-precision methods quantify depth, sensitivity, and heterogeneous allocation effects (Blumenfeld et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2020; Savarese et al., 2022). Per-tensor analyses and integer programs contain the dynamic-range-squared times 4−b4^{-b} distortion law and resource-constrained bit allocation (Chen et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2021). Practical large language model (LLM) quantization uses outlier handling, second-order rounding, activation rescaling, and data-dependent discrepancy control (Dettmers et al., 2022; Frantar et al., 2023; Xiao et al., 2023; Chee et al., 2025). Precision-aware scaling studies measure how these effects change with model size (Dettmers and Zettlemoyer, 2023; Kumar et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026); kernel-regime analysis establishes width-dependent convergence for 1-bit networks (Daliri et al., 2025). Our finite-precision analysis composes local numerical distortion with finite-sample uncertainty and the learned-state budget. For the specified computational graph, it also quantifies the arithmetic cost associated with the required precision.

Minimax generalization and attention optimization.

Worst-case neural-network theory controls function classes through Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension, pseudo-dimension, norms, margins, and covering numbers (Bartlett et al., 2019; Bartlett et al., 2017). Compression and description-length analyses relate concise predictors to generalization, including probably approximately correct (PAC)–Bayes bounds (Arora et al., 2018; Daniely and Granot, 2019; Lotfi et al., 2022). Distribution-specific minimax theory ties rates to compositional smoothness, Besov regularity, or intrinsic dimension (Schmidt-Hieber, 2020; Suzuki, 2019; Nakada and Imaizumi, 2020). Our statistical result follows this distribution-specific approach, with held-out autoregressive cross-entropy and an arbitrary finite learned state.

For sequence models, norm-based Transformer bounds, analyses of Markov next-token prediction, dependent-token pretraining, and nearly tight sample complexity address generalization under architecture or dependence (Trauger and Tewari, 2024; Yüksel and Flammarion, 2025; Li et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). Attention optimization studies max-margin token selection, retrieval learning, and frequency-dependent associative memory (Ataee Tarzanagh et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Cabannes et al., 2024). Structure-aware preconditioning gives a data–compute law for Gaussian softmax regression under an expected empirical-gradient oracle (Goel et al., 2026); other softmax-regression objectives admit efficient gradient methods with structured output constraints (Chu et al., 2024). Theory for prefix tuning and next-step forecasting identifies how attention training and its generalization depend on the learned representation (Liang et al., 2025; Ke et al., 2025). Complementary work asks which token state can be removed while preserving attention or long-context prediction: sparse approximation controls attention-matrix error, while parallel and value-aware compressors allocate a limited context state (Deng et al., 2024; Xiong et al., 2025; Yang and Li, 2026). We count the samples used to learn the relevant candidate and its prediction parameter, then the bits used to retain the fitted state. Appendix A gives the detailed comparison of the statistical, representational, and computational settings.

We first define the source and finite-state value-estimation problem; Section 4 additionally learns the relevant route.

3.2 Why Separate Marginals Cannot Identify Scaling

A fixed amount of predictive energy is harder to learn and retain when it is spread across more independent coordinates. Imagine two lists: the total energy assigned to each group and the number of independent coordinates in each group. A marginal descriptor retains these lists but forgets which energy goes with which dimension. We compare two assignments of the same lists: concentrate the high energies in one-coordinate groups, or spread them across the larger groups. The next theorem makes this comparison exact at every dyadic level, a level indexed by an integer ℓ\ell with group counts proportional to 2ℓ2^{\ell}.

Theorem 3.3 (Same block marginals, different scaling laws; informal version of Theorem C.6).

For every χ,γ>0\chi,\gamma>0, there are two positive-conditional-entropy causal-retrieval sources with exactly the same block-energy multiset and the same block-dimension multiset at every dyadic level. They differ only in the pairing. All displayed dimensions in this construction are rounded upward to integers. With the common fixed-KK route revealed,

ℜeasy(n,B)≍n−χ/(1+χ)+B−χ,\mathfrak{R}_{\rm easy}(n,B)\asymp n^{-\chi/(1+\chi)}+B^{-\chi},

whereas

ℜhard(n,B)≍n−χ/(1+χ+γ)+B−χ/(1+γ).\mathfrak{R}_{\rm hard}(n,B)\asymp n^{-\chi/(1+\chi+\gamma)}+B^{-\chi/(1+\gamma)}.

At dyadic level ℓ\ell, both sources have 2ℓ2^{\ell} high- and low-energy blocks with energies proportional to 2−(1+χ)​ℓ2^{-(1+\chi)\ell} and 2−(1+χ+δ)​ℓ2^{-(1+\chi+\delta)\ell}, and 2ℓ2^{\ell} copies each of dimensions 11 and 2γ​ℓ2^{\gamma\ell}. Choose δ>γ​χ\delta>\gamma\chi. The easy source pairs high energy with dimension one; the hard source pairs it with dimension 2γ​ℓ2^{\gamma\ell}. Thus both block marginals agree exactly, not merely asymptotically.

A component with block-energy exponent ss and dimension exponent gg has spectral tail index (1+g)/(1+s+g)(1+g)/(1+s+g). The high-energy component therefore has index 1/(1+χ)1/(1+\chi) in the easy source and (1+γ)/(1+χ+γ)(1+\gamma)/(1+\chi+\gamma) in the hard source; the condition on δ\delta makes the low-energy component lower order. Applying Corollary 3.2 yields all four exponents. The full construction and converse are in Appendix I.

Pairing changes the coordinate-energy distribution while preserving both block marginals. This is the information a scaling descriptor must retain; Equation 3.4 recovers it from the integrated tail.

4 Learning the Causal Self-Attention Predictor

The value theorem reveals the relevant coordinate. We now learn how to select it from the candidate tokens, then learn its prediction parameter. Training has two stages: route calibration (Stage A) followed by value learning (Stage V). Both use exact-arithmetic stochastic gradient descent (SGD); their sample and state costs are accounted for separately.

From a route table to query–key attention.

Let xq,xs∈ℝdx_{q},x_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be the query token and candidate token at position ss. Their fixed embeddings include orthogonal address blocks: PQ∈ℝK×dP_{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d} extracts the query row and PC∈ℝK×dP_{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times d} extracts the candidate position, so PQ​xq=eqP_{Q}x_{q}=e_{q} and PC​xs=esP_{C}x_{s}=e_{s}, where ese_{s} is the ss-th standard basis vector. Write dh≥Kd_{h}\geq K for the attention-head dimension. An isometric embedding J∈ℝdh×KJ\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times K}, satisfying J⊤​J=IKJ^{\top}J=I_{K}, places these addresses in the head. The trainable matrix A∈ℝK×KA\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K} stores one score for each query–position pair. Define the fixed key map and trainable query map by

WK=dh​J​PC,WQ​(A)=J​A⊤​PQ,⟨WQ​(A)​xq,WK​xs⟩dh=Aq​s.W_{K}=\sqrt{d_{h}}JP_{C},\qquad W_{Q}(A)=JA^{\top}P_{Q},\qquad\frac{\langle W_{Q}(A)x_{q},W_{K}x_{s}\rangle}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}=A_{qs}. (4.1)
Proposition 4.1 (Exact query–key realization; informal version of Proposition C.3).

With a strict causal mask over the KK preceding candidates, Equation 4.1 exactly realizes the route scores and attention. Fix WKW_{K} and train only WQW_{Q}’s query-address block. Euclidean SGD then gives the same AA update, attended feature, and output-vector gradient.

The fixed embedding, key projection, and value extraction contain neither the unknown route nor the unknown logits. Those quantities enter only the trained query-address block and output coordinates.

Learning the route.

For a fixed query row, calibration increases the matching score relative to its distractors. Zero initialization keeps the distractor scores equal. Their common gap from the matching score is the margin βt\beta_{t} after tt visits to that row; δt\delta_{t} is the total attention probability on incorrect candidates. The following result quantifies how calibration reduces this leakage.

Proposition 4.2 (Online routing dynamics; informal version of Proposition C.4).

For K≥2K\geq 2, zero initialization and softmax cross-entropy steps of size 0<η≤10<\eta\leq 1 give the margin and distractor mass after tt row visits:

βt+1=βt+η​Keβt+K−1,δt=K−1eβt+K−1.\beta_{t+1}=\beta_{t}+\eta\frac{K}{e^{\beta_{t}}+K-1},\qquad\delta_{t}=\frac{K-1}{e^{\beta_{t}}+K-1}.

After bK=Θη​(log⁡(e​K))b_{K}=\Theta_{\eta}(\log(eK)) visits, δt≍η[1+(t−bK)+]−1\delta_{t}\asymp_{\eta}[1+(t-b_{K})_{+}]^{-1}. For SAS_{A} independent calibration blocks and a held-out row,

𝔯K​(SA)=𝔼⁡[δN2],N∼Binomial⁡(SA,1/K).\mathfrak{r}_{K}(S_{A})=\mathbb{E}[\delta_{N}^{2}],\quad N\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(S_{A},1/K).

For 0<ε≤1/160<\varepsilon\leq 1/16, the time to 𝔯K≤ε\mathfrak{r}_{K}\leq\varepsilon is Θη(K{ε−1/2+log(eK)})\Theta_{\eta}(K\{\varepsilon^{-1/2}+\log(eK)\}); at K=1K=1, leakage and calibration cost vanish.

Learning and storing the values.

After calibration, we freeze the route and fit an output vector on An={i:qi≥n−1}A_{n}=\{i:q_{i}\geq n^{-1}\}. This active set contains coordinates whose energy is large enough to resolve at sample size nn. The natural box is 𝒲=∏i∈An[−Ri,Ri]\mathcal{W}=\prod_{i\in A_{n}}[-R_{i},R_{i}]; output-vector entries outside AnA_{n} are fixed at zero. The attended feature hth_{t} contains the attention-weighted coordinate indicators restricted to AnA_{n}. Let μsgd=916​min|z|≤R​σ′​(z)>0\mu_{\rm sgd}=\frac{9}{16}\min_{|z|\leq R}\sigma^{\prime}(z)>0 be the step-size constant used in the formal theorem. Starting from w1=0w_{1}=0, use ηt=2/[μsgd​(t+1)]\eta_{t}=2/[\mu_{\rm sgd}(t+1)] and return w¯n=2​∑t=1nt​wt/[n⁡(n+1)]\bar{w}_{n}=2\sum_{t=1}^{n}tw_{t}/[n(n+1)]. If AnA_{n} is empty, return zero. Projection Π𝒲D\Pi_{\mathcal{W}}^{D} uses the frequency-weighted norm ‖v‖D2=∑i∈Anpi​vi2\|v\|_{D}^{2}=\sum_{i\in A_{n}}p_{i}v_{i}^{2}. On the active coordinates, DD is restricted to AnA_{n}, and the update is

wt+1=Π𝒲D​[wt−ηt​D−1​{σ⁡(wt⊤​ht)−Yt}​ht],D=diag⁡(p).w_{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{W}}^{D}\!\left[w_{t}-\eta_{t}D^{-1}\{\sigma(w_{t}^{\top}h_{t})-Y_{t}\}h_{t}\right],\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(p). (4.2)

The final vector is encoded in coordinatewise scalar formats using BVB_{V} value-state bits. The format-range ratio κi\kappa_{i} compares its stored range with the logit radius RiR_{i}; unit ratios recover the representation problem of Section 3. We write F^\widehat{F} for the resulting causal predictor and ℛθ​(F^)\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(\widehat{F}) for its population cross-entropy on a complete prediction block. The term ℰarithmetic\mathcal{E}_{\rm arithmetic} accounts for deployment arithmetic error under the formal theorem’s numerical assumptions.

Theorem 4.3 (Causal self-attention realization; informal version of Theorem C.5).

The weighted-average SGD with scalar formats in Theorem C.5 satisfies

𝔼[ℛθ(F^)−ℒ∞]≲R,K,ηΦμ(n−1)+Dq,κfmt(BV)+𝔯K(SA)+ℰarithmetic,\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(\widehat{F})-\mathcal{L}_{\infty}]\lesssim_{R,K,\eta}\Phi_{\mu}(n^{-1})+D^{\rm fmt}_{q,\kappa}(B_{V})+\mathfrak{r}_{K}(S_{A})+\mathcal{E}_{\rm arithmetic}, (4.3)

where BVB_{V} is the value-state budget and κi≥1\kappa_{i}\geq 1 the public format-range ratio, with

Dq,κfmt​(BV)=infbi≥0,∑ibi≤BV∑iqi​min⁡{1,κi2​2−2​bi}.D^{\rm fmt}_{q,\kappa}(B_{V})=\inf_{b_{i}\geq 0,\,\sum_{i}b_{i}\leq B_{V}}\sum_{i}q_{i}\min\{1,\kappa_{i}^{2}2^{-2b_{i}}\}.

For κi=1\kappa_{i}=1, this is Φμ​(τBV)\Phi_{\mu}(\tau_{B_{V}}), and the core surface holds at total budget BB for power-law spectra, fixed KK, o⁡(B)o(B) routing bits and lower-order routing/arithmetic errors.

Conditioned on the route, output risk is strongly convex on fitted coordinates in the frequency-weighted norm; preconditioning balances their learning rates. Appendix B gives gradient, state, and format details.

The total resources.

Write BAB_{A} for the bits encoding the route, so total learned state is B=BV+BAB=B_{V}+B_{A}, and total training blocks are N=n+SAN=n+S_{A}. Let q(r)q_{(r)} list coordinate energies in decreasing order, with decay exponent ξ>0\xi>0. Charging both stages preserves the leading resource exponents: for q(r)≍r−(1+ξ)q_{(r)}\asymp r^{-(1+\xi)}, fixed KK, unit midpoint formats and the deployment-error condition in Proposition S.1, risk ε\varepsilon is achieved with N=n+SA=O(ε−(1+ξ)/ξ)N=n+S_{A}=O(\varepsilon^{-(1+\xi)/\xi}) total blocks and B=BV+BA=O(ε−1/ξ)B=B_{V}+B_{A}=O(\varepsilon^{-1/\xi}) total learned bits. Calibration blocks and route-state bits are lower-order terms.

5 Adaptive Representation and Finite-Precision Realization

Two representation questions remain after the resource law. How should bits be allocated when the energy decay is unknown? How accurately does a finite-precision attention network evaluate the retained parameters? The first result constructs an estimator and a storage schedule; the second maps supplied parameters to prediction error after numerical evaluation. Here scalar coordinates are indexed by jj, and Δj\Delta_{j} denotes the radius written RiR_{i} in Section 3. The loss ℒθ​(f)\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(f) is the same population cross-entropy.

Adaptive representation.

Theorem 5.1 (Adaptation with a known ordering; informal version of Theorem H.1).

Fix 0<χmin≤χmax<∞0<\chi_{\min}\leq\chi_{\max}<\infty, and suppose the canonical mode order is known. Assume qj≍j−(1+χ)q_{j}\asymp j^{-(1+\chi)} with common comparison constants and unknown χ∈[χmin,χmax]\chi\in[\chi_{\min},\chi_{\max}]. For every n,B∈ℕn,B\in\mathbb{N}, one clipped likelihood estimator and one deterministic integer bit schedule, both independent of χ\chi, satisfy simultaneously throughout this interval

supθj∈[−Δj,Δj]𝔼θ[ℒθ(f^)−ℒθ(θ)]≲n−χ/(1+χ)+B−χ.\sup_{\theta_{j}\in[-\Delta_{j},\Delta_{j}]}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(\widehat{f})-\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(\theta)\right]\lesssim n^{-\chi/(1+\chi)}+B^{-\chi}. (5.1)

Choose A>χmax/2A>\chi_{\max}/2 and the largest prefix mm satisfying

bj=⌊A​log2⁡(m/j)⌋+(j≤m),∑j≤mbj≤B.b_{j}=\left\lfloor A\log_{2}(m/j)\right\rfloor_{+}\quad(j\leq m),\qquad\sum_{j\leq m}b_{j}\leq B. (5.2)

Then m≍Bm\asymp B, and both quantization and omitted-tail errors are O⁡(m−χ)O(m^{-\chi}) uniformly over the exponent interval. The logarithmic schedule spends most bits on the leading coordinates while matching the tail error for every allowed decay rate.

Finite-precision self-attention.

We construct a network that evaluates a supplied logit table for the first MM coordinates and uses zero for the rest. Here MM is the retained prefix length, t⋆t_{\star} is the matching candidate position, and β≥0\beta\geq 0 controls the matching attention score. The candidate’s mode label jtj_{t} identifies its scalar table entry. Use public basis addresses at∈ℝKa_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}, mode vectors ej(M)=eje_{j}^{(M)}=e_{j} for j≤Mj\leq M and zero otherwise, and d=K+M+1d=K+M+1. Candidate and query tokens are xt=(at,ejt(M),0)x_{t}=(a_{t},e_{j_{t}}^{(M)},0) and xq=(at⋆,0,1)x_{q}=(a_{t_{\star}},0,1). The fixed-key construction in Proposition 4.1 gives

⟨WQ​xq,WK​xt⟩dh=β⁡⟨at⋆,at⟩.\frac{\langle W_{Q}x_{q},W_{K}x_{t}\rangle}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}=\beta\langle a_{t_{\star}},a_{t}\rangle. (5.3)

With the value projection onto mode coordinates, a strict causal mask, and an output vector ww supported only on those coordinates,

hq=∑t=1Kαt​e¯jt(M),αt=exp(β𝟏{t=t⋆})eβ+K−1,z=w⊤​hq,h_{q}=\sum_{t=1}^{K}\alpha_{t}\bar{e}_{j_{t}}^{(M)},\qquad\alpha_{t}=\frac{\exp(\beta\mathbf{1}\{t=t_{\star}\})}{e^{\beta}+K-1},\qquad z=w^{\top}h_{q}, (5.4)

where e¯j(M)=(0,ej(M),0)\bar{e}_{j}^{(M)}=(0,e_{j}^{(M)},0). Write wjmode=wK+jw_{j}^{\rm mode}=w_{K+j}, and set ϑj=wjmode\vartheta_{j}=w_{j}^{\rm mode} for j≤Mj\leq M and ϑj=0\vartheta_{j}=0 otherwise.

The numerical calculation below uses unit roundoff uu, an upper bound on the relative error of the listed scalar operations. Its four error terms respectively measure selecting a distractor, arithmetic rounding, storing the retained logits, and predicting omitted coordinates with zero.

Theorem 5.2 (Finite-precision realization; informal version of Theorem J.1).

Fix K,M≥1K,M\geq 1, R<∞R<\infty, β≥0\beta\geq 0, and the construction above.

  1. 1.

    In exact arithmetic, if |wjmode|≤R\lvert w_{j}^{\rm mode}\rvert\leq R for every j∈[M]j\in[M], then a query whose matching candidate has any mode j≥1j\geq 1 satisfies

    |z−ϑj|≤2​R​(K−1)​e−β.\lvert z-\vartheta_{j}\rvert\leq 2R(K-1)e^{-\beta}. (5.5)
  2. 2.

    Set wjmode=θjw_{j}^{\rm mode}=\theta_{j} for j∈[M]j\in[M] and store it with bj∈ℕ0b_{j}\in\mathbb{N}_{0} bits on [−Δj,Δj][-\Delta_{j},\Delta_{j}]. Assume stable max-shifted softmax with exactly representable shifted scores 0,−β0,-\beta and an exponent range containing their exponentials. Exponentials, multiplications, and divisions have relative error at most uu; sums use balanced pairwise accumulation. For the resulting predictor ffpf_{\rm fp}, if (⌈log2⁡K⌉+4)​u≤1/4(\lceil\log_{2}K\rceil+4)u\leq 1/4, then the held-out excess cross-entropy obeys

    ℒθ​(ffp)−ℒ∞≤CR​{(K−1)2​e−2​β+u2​(1+log⁡K)2+∑j=1Mqj​2−2​bj+∑j>Mqj}.\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(f_{\rm fp})-\mathcal{L}_{\infty}\leq C_{R}\left\{(K-1)^{2}e^{-2\beta}+u^{2}(1+\log K)^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{M}q_{j}2^{-2b_{j}}+\sum_{j>M}q_{j}\right\}. (5.6)
  3. 3.

    Within the separable scalar-table representation in which coordinate jj has at most 2bj2^{b_{j}} values, the bit-dependent term in Equation 5.6 is tight up to constants.

Here and below, CRC_{R} depends only on the logit bound RR.

The bound separates routing, arithmetic, quantization, and omitted energy. Pairwise summation gives logarithmic dependence on KK in arithmetic error before squaring. This result evaluates supplied logits; Theorem 4.3 controls their learning. Dense storage accounting and proofs appear in Appendices B, H, and J.

6 Bit Complexity and Compute–Precision Scaling

Representation accuracy is useful only if the chosen arithmetic can preserve it. This section separates the precision needed as the represented prefix grows, the work of a specified dense graph, and the savings from lowering precision at a fixed shape.

Error and cost as model size grows.

Here MM is the number of represented scalar modes, bb is arithmetic precision, and χ>0\chi>0 is the model-error decay exponent. The operation exponent f≥0f\geq 0 describes per-block work; ν≥0\nu\geq 0 describes how scalar-operation cost grows with bit width. The function κ⁡(M)\kappa(M) amplifies stored perturbations into prediction error. Suppose representing MM modes has error Θ⁡(M−χ)\Theta(M^{-\chi}), each processed block costs Θ⁡(Mf)\Theta(M^{f}) scalar operations, Θ⁡(M1+χ)\Theta(M^{1+\chi}) blocks are necessary and sufficient, a bb-bit operation costs Θ⁡(bν)\Theta(b^{\nu}), and stored perturbation 2−b2^{-b} produces error Θ⁡(κ​(M)2​2−2​b)\Theta(\kappa(M)^{2}2^{-2b}). Under these two-sided assumptions, ℛ⁡(C)\mathcal{R}(C) is the best held-out risk at arithmetic budget CC.

Counting a dense forward–backward pass.

To relate these abstract costs to an implementation, fix a conventional Transformer graph. Its matrix arithmetic and softmax arithmetic can use different precisions, denoted bmmb_{\rm mm} and bsmb_{\rm sm}. For a dense Transformer with sequence length ℓ\ell, width dd, feed-forward width mffm_{\rm ff}, HH heads, and LL layers, its conventional forward–backward arithmetic is, up to constants,

L⁡[(ℓ​d2+ℓ​d​mff+ℓ2​d)​𝖬​(bmm)+H​ℓ2​𝖲​(bsm)].L\!\left[(\ell d^{2}+\ell dm_{\rm ff}+\ell^{2}d)\mathsf{M}(b_{\rm mm})+H\ell^{2}\mathsf{S}(b_{\rm sm})\right].

Here 𝖬⁡(bmm)\mathsf{M}(b_{\rm mm}) and 𝖲⁡(bsm)\mathsf{S}(b_{\rm sm}) are the bit-operation costs of a matrix multiply–accumulate and a softmax scalar operation at their respective precisions. This forward–backward count excludes optimizer updates. Recomputation reduces saved attention state while preserving the dense arithmetic order.

Theorem 6.1 (Precision-aware compute phases; informal version of Theorem M.1).

For the two-sided risk–cost family of Theorem M.1, with χ>0\chi>0, f,ν≥0f,\nu\geq 0, and n⁡(M)≍M1+χn(M)\asymp M^{1+\chi}:

  1. 1.

    If 1≲κ⁡(M)≲Mρ1\lesssim\kappa(M)\lesssim M^{\rho}, then the least model-error-matching precision is b=Θ⁡(log⁡M)b=\Theta(\log M), and

    ℛ(C)−ℒ∞≍C−χ/(f+1+χ)(logC)χ​ν/(f+1+χ)\mathcal{R}(C)-\mathcal{L}_{\infty}\asymp C^{-\chi/(f+1+\chi)}(\log C)^{\chi\nu/(f+1+\chi)} (6.1)

    up to other slowly varying factors specified in the assumptions.

  2. 2.

    If κ⁡(M)=exp⁡(Θ⁡(Mλ))\kappa(M)=\exp(\Theta(M^{\lambda})), λ>0\lambda>0, then b=Θ⁡(Mλ)b=\Theta(M^{\lambda}), and the loss exponent is χ/(f+1+χ+λ​ν)\chi/(f+1+\chi+\lambda\nu).

  3. 3.

    If qj≍j−(1+χ)q_{j}\asymp j^{-(1+\chi)}, adaptive per-mode precision has error Θ⁡(B−χ)\Theta(B^{-\chi}), whereas a uniform-width prefix has optimal error

    Θ⁡((B/log⁡B)−χ).\Theta((B/\log B)^{-\chi}). (6.2)

Each converse uses the representation, operation set, storage layout, and bit-operation cost specified above.

The polynomial-conditioning exponent ρ\rho in this theorem describes κ⁡(M)\kappa(M), independently of the spectral tail index used in Section 3. Matching numerical error to M−χM^{-\chi} requires

b≥log2⁡κ⁡(M)+χ2​log2​M−O⁡(1).b\geq\log_{2}\kappa(M)+\frac{\chi}{2}\log_{2}M-O(1). (6.3)

Savings at a fixed shape.

We now hold model dimensions fixed and change only the numerical formats. This compares two implementations of the same graph. Retained high-precision work produces an Amdahl-type ceiling: reducing one part’s cost leaves the other part unchanged. At fixed shape, let G,SG,S count matrix and softmax operations, ν,νsm\nu,\nu_{\rm sm} their precision-cost exponents, QQ the quantized scalar count, and RhpR_{\rm hp} the retained high-precision bits. Lowering the matrix and stored-scalar precision from baseline b0b_{0} to bb gives

BitOpsRatio=G​b0ν+S​bsmνsmG​bν+S​bsmνsm,Compressionbit=Q​b0+RhpQ​b+Rhp.\operatorname{BitOpsRatio}=\frac{Gb_{0}^{\nu}+Sb_{\rm sm}^{\nu_{\rm sm}}}{Gb^{\nu}+Sb_{\rm sm}^{\nu_{\rm sm}}},\qquad\operatorname{Compression}_{\rm bit}=\frac{Qb_{0}+R_{\rm hp}}{Qb+R_{\rm hp}}.

In this calculation, QQ counts quantized scalars rather than query rows, and SS counts softmax operations rather than learned states. Ratios larger than one denote reduced bit operations or storage. Thus fixed-precision softmax, master weights, optimizer state, or saved high-precision activations can dominate even when matrix precision falls.

Appendix B derives the dense forward–backward count, storage requirements, and precision–risk trade-off.

7 Experiments

Experimental design.

We test spectral risk, coupling, and attention learning. Training and held-out blocks are independent, and comparisons are paired by seed or evaluation item. The fixed-source synthetic studies evaluate excess cross-entropy (CE), the loss above the source’s Bayes predictor and use 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap intervals over paired seeds. Complementary mini-batch and terminal-iterate studies test robustness to the learning implementation. Appendices Q and R specify the algorithms, evaluation units, and uncertainty procedures.

Data–memory surface and exponent agreement.

Does the same source statistic organize both resources in the stated learner? We fix four sources, each with 256 energy groups rather than 256 training examples, and cross five sample budgets with six value-state budgets. Each sample budget restarts the theorem’s weighted-average SGD in FP64; all state budgets encode that same fitted vector. Full-source excess CE follows the resource ordering of GμG_{\mu} for both SGD and the oracle-coordinate estimator (Figure 2). Unbinned risk-to-GμG_{\mu} ratios reveal the remaining finite-resource variation (Figure 11). The six-profile exponent grid and candidate-count replication appear in Appendix P, alongside the spectral slopes (Table 4(b)).

Same-marginal coupling.

Can identical block-energy and block-dimension marginals produce different data laws as well as different memory laws? On the same normalized dyadic source, the fitted easy/hard data exponents are 0.509/0.3390.509/0.339 for χ=1\chi=1 and 0.681/0.4890.681/0.489 for χ=2\chi=2, against predictions 1/2,1/31/2,1/3 and 2/3,1/22/3,1/2, respectively. Fits use the same last four sample budgets for all 16 seeds. Figure 3(a,d) shows every budget; panels (b,e) and Table 2(b) retain the complementary storage separation. Pairing changes both resource exponents, not just their constants.

Learned routing and interventions.

Routing experiments train routing and output parameters through the actual network forward map. Its 256 combinations of source profile, represented prefix, candidate count, and seed separately restart each learner at three nominal sample budgets and reuse fitted states across bit budgets. Routing leakage decreases with actual visits, and learned routing approaches the known-route learner while a frozen uniform route does not (Figure 3(c,f)). Tables 2(c) and 2(d) separates data, tail, routing, and format terms and changes routing, preconditioning, or precision one factor at a time. At the unit-bit-ratio setting in Appendix Table 3, learned and known routing yield 0.0191±0.00020.0191\pm 0.0002 and 0.0192±0.00020.0192\pm 0.0002 augmented loss, versus 0.0605±0.00080.0605\pm 0.0008 with a frozen route; these augmented losses include the common M−χM^{-\chi} proxy. Removing preconditioning gives 0.0230±0.00030.0230\pm 0.0003. The half-bit-ratio table reveals the uniform-precision penalty at a tighter memory budget, complementing this unit-bit-ratio comparison.

Stored formats and softmax precision.

We compare a shared quantization scale, scales per energy group or per coordinate, and adaptive bit widths. Three conditioning regimes vary the format-range amplification relative to logit radii. A softmax sweep records numerical format, underflow, and matching mass at K∈{8,32,128,512}K\in\{8,32,128,512\}. At eight bits, adaptive widths reduce format distortion to 7.82×10−107.82\times 10^{-10}, compared with 8.46×10−68.46\times 10^{-6} for uniform block widths and 1.08×10−51.08\times 10^{-5} for a shared scale. Appendix Figure 8 shows the format trade-off and retained high-precision work: bit allocation controls distortion, while the fraction quantized determines resource savings.

Profile robustness.

We test broken-power-law, logarithmically corrected, and perturbed-order profiles using each source’s exact finite spectrum. The empirical allocator uses fitted logits and counts to estimate energies, subtracting a sampling-noise correction. Known-energy allocation instead minimizes representation distortion using the true energies; uniform widths provide a second reference. Comparisons use eight paired seeds. Appendix R gives both objectives, distinct from the deterministic unknown-exponent schedule of Theorem 5.1. It retains the advantage over uniform allocation across the three displayed deviations (Appendix Figure 6).

Pretrained Transformers.

Weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) tests the deployment effect across six Pythia checkpoints at step143000. We compare tensor/channel 8-bit integer formats (INT8), 4-bit integer (INT4) round-to-nearest (RTN), and half-quadratic quantization (HQQ) with groups of 128 or 32 weights (g128/g32) against bfloat16 (BF16), using paired WikiText-103 windows and LAMBADA items. The HQQ-g32 penalty generally decreases with scale, except at 1.4B; the 2.8B LAMBADA interval includes zero (Table 2(a)). Appendix Figures 9 and 4(a) retain all formats and BF16 baselines. Softmax remains in 32-bit floating point (FP32), so the comparison isolates weight representation.

We additionally continue all six checkpoints along four nested WikiText-103 token budgets, using eight training seeds per model, and materialize group-128 2/3/4/6/8-bit and BF16 deployment packages. The complete scan separates model-scale and format effects (Figure 4(a–f)): 2/3-bit quantization causes the largest loss increases at 70M/160M, while the four larger models have substantially smaller penalties. Including 2-bit calibration yields fits within the specified [0,20][0,20]-nat prediction range at 410M–2.8B. At 70M/160M, the 2-bit losses exceed this range; the fitting procedure does not yield converged, in-range solutions. Each scale is fitted separately.

The sensitivity analysis fits 4/8-bit and BF16 validation configurations and holds out 6-bit plus the largest token budget. On untouched test windows, the additive response improves data-extrapolation root-mean-square error (RMSE) relative to the data-only fit at every scale. The reductions are 0.910​[0.871,0.944]0.910\,[0.871,0.944] for 70M and 0.380​[0.352,0.394]0.380\,[0.352,0.394] for 160M; the four larger models show smaller absolute improvements. For 6-bit interpolation, the additive response has higher RMSE at 70M/160M and lower RMSE at 410M–2.8B. Thus model scale changes both quantization sensitivity and the predictive value of a smooth joint-resource response. Appendix Figure 7 shows every format and budget with seed-level uncertainty; Tables 5 and 6 report the corresponding prediction errors for each model.

8 Conclusion

Finite data and finite learned memory resolve the same predictive-energy spectrum at different thresholds. For the causal source studied here, this gives minimax risk, scaling exponents, and a data–memory crossover. The complete curve identifies the positive spectrum, retaining information that a fitted exponent alone loses.

Energy–dimension pairing determines the spectrum: identical block marginals can conceal different data and memory laws. A masked query–key head learns the relevant route and values, connecting this statistical structure to attention. Adaptive allocation, finite-precision realization, and conditional compute laws quantify how the representation uses resources.

Experiments trace these mechanisms through spectral collapse, coupling, routing, and numerical precision. The organizing principle is the distribution of predictive information across independent coordinates: it explains both what data can reveal and what a finite predictor can retain.

APPENDIX

Appendix A Discussion, Scope, and Closest Precedents

One curve for two resources.

The central object is the spectrum of predictive energy per independent coordinate. Its integrated tail answers both what data cannot resolve and what a finite learned state cannot retain. Data evaluate it at resolution 1/n1/n; storage chooses a water level. The same-marginal construction shows why the energy–dimension pairing is indispensable.

Knowledge capacity as an inverse resource curve.

To express the information relation, place a fixed prior on the source parameters ZZ, including the route when it is unknown. Let SS be the learned state formed from training blocks, and let XX contain all candidates and the query of an independent held-out block. Conditional on (X,Z)(X,Z), the target YY is independent of the training state. Entropy and mutual information, denoted by HH and II, are measured in nats. The conditional mutual-information identity and the finite-state constraint give

H(Y∣X,S)−H(Y∣X,Z)=I(Y;Z∣X,S),I(Z;S)≤H(S)≤Blog2.H(Y\mid X,S)-H(Y\mid X,Z)=I(Y;Z\mid X,S),\qquad I(Z;S)\leq H(S)\leq B\log 2.

The first difference compares the Bayes predictive losses given the learned state and given the source parameters; a particular decoder can incur additional loss. The prior is used for this information comparison, whereas the main minimax theorem takes a worst case over fixed parameters. This identity places knowledge-capacity and prediction-risk laws on opposite directions of the same information path. Allen-Zhu and Li (Allen-Zhu and Li, 2025) turn factual generation loss into a lower bound on the information retained by model weights—a loss-to-bits question. Our minimax law turns nn observations and BB retained bits into the smallest held-out excess loss—a bits-to-risk question. Deterministic factual recall and positive-entropy prediction yield complementary geometries: the former prices discrete facts, while local KL curvature in the latter produces the coordinate distortion qi​2−2​biq_{i}2^{-2b_{i}}, reverse water filling, and the common spectrum. Frequency-ranked knowledge also yields data and model scaling under a compression model (Pan et al., 2025); here the paired predictive energies determine the complete finite-(n,B)(n,B) curve, and the same-marginal construction isolates the pairing information required for its exponents. Empirical capacity estimates (Allen-Zhu and Li, 2025; Morris et al., 2025) calibrate how efficiently a particular architecture stores information per parameter; the spectrum supplies the source-dependent risk curve to which such an architectural calibration can be attached. Sparse attention, prefix learning, and context compression (Liang et al., 2025; Deng et al., 2024; Xiong et al., 2025; Yang and Li, 2026) then connect the abstract state budget to the practical question of which predictive coordinates a Transformer should retain.

Learning the routing and value parameters.

Public addresses determine where comparisons occur, unknown routing is learned in the query projection, and unknown values are learned in the output coordinates. Fixing the key projection preserves the route-table scores and routing-gradient trajectory. This identifies the trainable parameters through which self-attention acquires the source’s predictive structure.

A hierarchy of resource laws.

The arbitrary-state lower bound applies to every learner with at most 2B2^{B} final value states. The routing lower bound belongs to the stated row-symmetric online trajectory; the format lower bound applies to the required stored interface; the bit-operation lower bound concerns the specified dense graph and arithmetic model. Each result identifies the cost of a distinct bottleneck and makes the progression from statistical information to numerical computation explicit.

From learning to finite-precision prediction.

The two-stage learning theorem trains routing and output coordinates using public coordinate frequencies, supervised calibration, and exact-arithmetic updates. The finite-precision theorem starts from supplied mode logits and quantifies their realization by the network; its converse concerns the separable scalar-table representation. The compute theorem studies precision allocation under a two-sided numerical response assumption. Together, these results form a three-step account of acquiring parameters, representing them numerically, and allocating arithmetic resources. A unified low-precision training theorem would complete this chain at the level of the optimization trajectory.

Precision in practical Transformer stacks.

The benefit of a low-bit matrix path depends on the fraction of storage and arithmetic it changes. FP32 softmax, accumulation, master weights, optimizer states, and saved activations contribute retained high-precision work. Streaming attention reduces retained state while preserving the dense arithmetic order. Device-level speedups are governed by the corresponding throughput and memory-traffic costs.

Open directions.

Three extensions would carry the spectrum principle into broader sequence models: jointly learning frequencies, ordering, queries, and keys; analyzing low-precision stochastic updates along the routing and value trajectories; and estimating predictive-energy spectra from unrestricted corpora. These directions turn the present exact source model into a program for predicting resource tradeoffs in learned representations.

Appendix B Extended Representation and Compute Results

This appendix gives the complete statements and derivations summarized in Sections 5 and 6.

B.1 Adaptive Schedule and Information Used

The schedule in Equation 5.2 knows the canonical index order and the interval [χmin,χmax][\chi_{\min},\chi_{\max}], but not χ\chi. It adapts to the decay rate while treating energy ordering as side information. Data-driven allocation with an unknown ordering is related to adaptive quantized Sobolev estimation (Zhu and Lafferty, 2018b); learning that ordering together with the bit schedule is a separate statistical problem. The full proof and restatement are in Appendix H.

B.2 Finite-Precision Forward Error and Storage

The matching attention weight in Equation 5.4 is α⋆=eβ/(eβ+K−1)\alpha_{\star}=e^{\beta}/(e^{\beta}+K-1). Since the output coordinates lie in [−R,R][-R,R], |z−ϑj⋆|≤2​R​(1−α⋆)≤2​R​(K−1)​e−β\lvert z-\vartheta_{j_{\star}}\rvert\leq 2R(1-\alpha_{\star})\leq 2R(K-1)e^{-\beta}. Uniformly quantizing [−Δj,Δj][-\Delta_{j},\Delta_{j}] with 2bj2^{b_{j}} values gives

|w~jmode−wjmode|≤2​Δj​2−bj.\lvert\widetilde{w}_{j}^{\rm mode}-w_{j}^{\rm mode}\rvert\leq 2\Delta_{j}2^{-b_{j}}. (B.1)

For arithmetic error, let uu be the unit roundoff of the scalar operations. Max shifting produces unnormalized weights in {1,e−β}\{1,e^{-\beta}\}. Balanced pairwise summation has depth h=⌈log2⁡K⌉h=\lceil\log_{2}K\rceil; put γh=h​u/(1−h​u)\gamma_{h}=hu/(1-hu). Positive pairwise summation incurs relative error at most γh\gamma_{h}. Composing exponential, denominator, and division errors gives, when (h+4)​u≤1/4(h+4)u\leq 1/4,

∥α^−α∥1≤8​(h+4)​u.\lVert\widehat{\alpha}-\alpha\rVert_{1}\leq 8(h+4)u. (B.2)

The final weighted sum can have mixed signs, so an absolute bound is needed:

|fl⁡(w~⊤​α^)−w~⊤​α|≤CR​u​(1+log⁡K).\lvert\operatorname{fl}(\widetilde{w}^{\top}\widehat{\alpha})-\widetilde{w}^{\top}\alpha\rvert\leq C_{R}u(1+\log K). (B.3)

The absolute bound also handles cancellation. Combining routing, quantization, and arithmetic errors, squaring and averaging over the mode, and applying bounded log-loss curvature yields Equation 5.6, including the unrepresented tail. The detailed proof and restatement of Theorem 5.2 are in Appendix J.

Learned state versus physical storage.

Here d=K+M+1d=K+M+1 is the token width of the particular realization in Section 5, with MM retained scalar output coordinates. If the score matrix, value projection, and output head are dense arrays, their physical scalar-slot count is

N=2​d2+d.N=2d^{2}+d. (B.4)

Only the MM output coordinates depend on the source, and their description length is ∑j=1Mbj\sum_{j=1}^{M}b_{j}. Thus NN, MM, and BB are different resources even in this fixed-depth, one-head realization with public orthogonal addresses. The finite-precision theorem initializes those coordinates with supplied logits; Theorem 4.3 separately analyzes gradient training of routing and output values.

B.3 Forward–Backward Bit Complexity

Consider eager, non-checkpointed reverse-mode differentiation (standard backpropagation) through a dense Transformer with sequence length ℓ\ell, hidden width dd, feed-forward width mffm_{\rm ff}, HH attention heads whose widths sum to dd, and LL layers. Matrix multiplications use a format indexed by bmmb_{\rm mm}, the stable max-shifted softmax uses compute precision bsmb_{\rm sm}, and a materialized attention probability uses bstb_{\rm st} storage bits. The index bmmb_{\rm mm} determines all operand, output, and accumulator widths in this format family. Let 𝖬⁡(bmm)\mathsf{M}(b_{\rm mm}) be the bit-operation cost of one such multiply–accumulate. Let 𝖲⁡(bsm)\mathsf{S}(b_{\rm sm}) be the amortized per-attention-entry cost of stable softmax and its reverse-mode Jacobian–vector product, including exponentials, reductions, division, and pointwise arithmetic. We assume normalization, activation, and cast costs per entry do not asymptotically exceed these matrix and softmax costs. We do not count the optimizer update. This conventional query/key/value/output stack is a separate computational graph from the smaller realization in Section 5. Let bwb_{w} and bab_{a} denote aggregate bits per stored weight and activation slot at peak memory, and let Memhp\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm hp} denote retained high-precision state.

Lemma B.1 (Transformer forward–backward bit complexity; informal version of Lemma K.1).

For the graph above, with positive dimensions and conventional dense matrix multiplication,

BitOpsfb≍L⁡[(ℓ​d2+ℓ​d​mff+ℓ2​d)​𝖬​(bmm)+H​ℓ2​𝖲​(bsm)].\operatorname{BitOps}_{\rm fb}\asymp L\Bigl[\bigl(\ell d^{2}+\ell dm_{\rm ff}+\ell^{2}d\bigr)\mathsf{M}(b_{\rm mm})+H\ell^{2}\mathsf{S}(b_{\rm sm})\Bigr]. (B.5)
Memfb≍bw​L​(d2+d​mff)+ba​L​ℓ​(d+mff)+bst​L​H​ℓ2+Memhp.\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm fb}\asymp b_{w}L(d^{2}+dm_{\rm ff})+b_{a}L\ell(d+m_{\rm ff})+b_{\rm st}LH\ell^{2}+\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm hp}. (B.6)

The memory Memfb\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm fb} is measured in bits. The values bwb_{w}, bab_{a}, and bstb_{\rm st} count aggregate bits per logical weight, activation, and saved-attention slot at peak memory; they include any same-shaped gradient or backward-workspace buffer materialized by this eager implementation. The term Memhp\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm hp} contains master weights, optimizer state, and all other explicitly retained high-precision data. A streaming, recomputing attention implementation replaces the quadratic attention state saved for backward by linear online-softmax state plus temporary tile workspace, while leaving the dense attention arithmetic order unchanged.

The three matrix terms in Equation B.5 come respectively from the input/output projections, the two feed-forward projections, and the score–value attention products. Reverse mode performs two matrix products for each forward matrix product, so it changes constants rather than orders. For a softmax row pp and incoming vector vv, its derivative is applied as (diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤)​v=p⊙(v−⟨p,v⟩​𝟏)(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\top})v=p\odot(v-\langle p,v\rangle\mathbf{1}). Thus the Jacobian–vector product costs Θ⁡(H​ℓ2)\Theta(H\ell^{2}), without forming an ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell Jacobian for every row. The proof and a shape-by-shape operation count are in Appendix K.

B.4 The Compute–Precision Pareto Law

Let MM denote the number of represented modes. Under a specified shape schedule (ℓ,d,mff,H,L)​(M)(\ell,d,m_{\rm ff},H,L)(M), Lemma B.1 gives G⁡(M)≍L⁡(ℓ​d2+ℓ​d​mff+ℓ2​d)G(M)\asymp L(\ell d^{2}+\ell dm_{\rm ff}+\ell^{2}d) and S⁡(M)≍L​H​ℓ2S(M)\asymp LH\ell^{2}. We write G⁡(M)≍MgG(M)\asymp M^{g} for quantizable matrix work and S⁡(M)≍MsS(M)\asymp M^{s} for softmax work, where g,s≥0g,s\geq 0. Reaching model error M−χM^{-\chi} requires n⁡(M)≍M1+χn(M)\asymp M^{1+\chi} independent blocks. Let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote held-out excess risk, and let κmm\kappa_{\rm mm} and κsm\kappa_{\rm sm} measure how matrix and softmax rounding errors are amplified. We assume the following two-sided error and cost relations, which separate effective matrix precision bb from effective softmax precision bsmb_{\rm sm}:

ℰ⁡(M,b,bsm)≍M−χ+κmm​(M)2​2−2​b+κsm​(M)2​2−2​bsm.\mathcal{E}(M,b,b_{\rm sm})\asymp M^{-\chi}+\kappa_{\rm mm}(M)^{2}2^{-2b}+\kappa_{\rm sm}(M)^{2}2^{-2b_{\rm sm}}. (B.7)
C≍M1+χ​[G⁡(M)​bν+S⁡(M)​bsmνsm].C\asymp M^{1+\chi}\left[G(M)b^{\nu}+S(M)b_{\rm sm}^{\nu_{\rm sm}}\right]. (B.8)

The exponents ν,νsm≥0\nu,\nu_{\rm sm}\geq 0 belong to the stated arithmetic model. The abstract format family has total width proportional to its effective precision, equivalently unit roundoff Θ⁡(2−b)\Theta(2^{-b}); concrete floating-point formats are discussed separately below.

Theorem B.2 (Compute–precision Pareto law; informal version of Theorem L.1).

Assume Equations B.7 and B.8, κmm​(M)≍Mr\kappa_{\rm mm}(M)\asymp M^{r}, and κsm​(M)≍Mrsm\kappa_{\rm sm}(M)\asymp M^{r_{\rm sm}}, with all displayed relations two-sided and r,rsm≥0r,r_{\rm sm}\geq 0. For the specified dense graph, H≤dH\leq d implies G≳SG\gtrsim S and hence g≥sg\geq s. Item 3 concerns general operation counts satisfying the same two-sided relations; items 1, 2, and 4 apply to both settings.

  1. 1.

    The smallest matrix precision that keeps matrix rounding at the model error is

    bmatch​(M)=(r+χ2)​log2​M+O⁡(1).b_{\rm match}(M)=\left(r+\frac{\chi}{2}\right)\log_{2}M+O(1). (B.9)
  2. 2.

    If the matrix term dominates the bracket in Equation B.8 at matched precisions—in particular in the case g≥sg\geq s when the remaining precision factors do not reverse that dominance—then

    infM,b,bsm:cost≤Cℰ≍C−χ/(1+χ+g)(logC)χ​ν/(1+χ+g),\inf_{M,b,b_{\rm sm}:\,\mathrm{cost}\leq C}\mathcal{E}\asymp C^{-\chi/(1+\chi+g)}(\log C)^{\chi\nu/(1+\chi+g)}, (B.10)

    up to other declared slowly varying factors.

  3. 3.

    For general operation counts, if s>gs>g, bsmb_{\rm sm} is fixed, and the softmax term dominates computation, then for budgets in the pre-floor range

    C1/(1+χ+s)≲22​bsm/(χ+2​rsm),C^{1/(1+\chi+s)}\lesssim 2^{2b_{\rm sm}/(\chi+2r_{\rm sm})},
    infM,b:cost≤Cℰ≍C−χ/(1+χ+s).\inf_{M,b:\,\mathrm{cost}\leq C}\mathcal{E}\asymp C^{-\chi/(1+\chi+s)}. (B.11)

    Reducing matrix precision cannot improve this leading exponent.

  4. 4.

    At fixed matrix precision bb, with softmax precision optimized, the model–rounding crossover and the infimum error over model scales are

    Mb≍22​b/(χ+2​r),ℰfloor(b)≍2−2χb/(χ+2r).M_{b}\asymp 2^{2b/(\chi+2r)},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{\rm floor}(b)\asymp 2^{-2\chi b/(\chi+2r)}. (B.12)

    A fixed bsmb_{\rm sm}-bit softmax similarly supports the scaling phase only while

    M≲22​bsm/(χ+2​rsm).M\lesssim 2^{2b_{\rm sm}/(\chi+2r_{\rm sm})}. (B.13)

The displayed two-sided risk and arithmetic assumptions define the class over which the infima and matching bounds are taken.

The theorem distinguishes increasing precision from fixed-precision deployment. Polynomial conditioning requires only logarithmically increasing precision, so adaptive precision changes a logarithmic factor, not the power exponent. Conversely, permanently fixing the precision creates a numerical floor. For a concrete 32-bit floating-point (FP32) softmax with unit roundoff usmu_{\rm sm}, provided the stated exponent-range and relative-error assumptions remain valid, Equation B.13 reads M≲usm−2/(χ+2rsm)M\lesssim u_{\rm sm}^{-2/(\chi+2r_{\rm sm})}; the total format width is not substituted for effective accuracy bits. Exponential conditioning, treated in Theorem 6.1, is the case in which precision itself creates a new power-law phase.

Limits imposed by high-precision work.

At a fixed model shape, lowering a matrix path from baseline precision b0b_{0} to bb gives the relative bit-operation count

BitOpsRatio=G​b0ν+S​bsmνsmG​bν+S​bsmνsm.\operatorname{BitOpsRatio}=\frac{Gb_{0}^{\nu}+Sb_{\rm sm}^{\nu_{\rm sm}}}{Gb^{\nu}+Sb_{\rm sm}^{\nu_{\rm sm}}}. (B.14)

If QQ stored scalars can be quantized and RhpR_{\rm hp} bits must remain at high precision, the corresponding storage ratio is

Compressionbit=Q​b0+RhpQ​b+Rhp.\operatorname{Compression}_{\rm bit}=\frac{Qb_{0}+R_{\rm hp}}{Qb+R_{\rm hp}}. (B.15)

These formulas expose the ceiling imposed by high-precision normalization, master weights, optimizer states, or saved activations. Actual graphics processor speed also depends on memory traffic, kernel support, and hardware throughput.

The two analytic consequences appear in Figure 1: its left panel shows the retained-high-precision ceiling in Equation B.14, and its right panel compares the three risk–cost regimes above.

The proofs follow the paper’s mechanism order: the spectral identities and their exponents, the query–key realization and online route, the network upper bound, and the same-marginal separation.

Throughout this appendix, ii indexes the scalar coordinates defined in Section 3. Their energies are qi=pi​Ri2q_{i}=p_{i}R_{i}^{2}, the spectrum is μ=∑iδqi\mu=\sum_{i}\delta_{q_{i}}, and Φμ​(t)=∑imin⁡{qi,t}\Phi_{\mu}(t)=\sum_{i}\min\{q_{i},t\}. The water level τB\tau_{B} is selected by the storage budget in that setup. Each restatement below uses the same objects as its corresponding main-text result.

Theorem C.1 (One spectrum controls data and memory; formal version of Theorem 3.1).

Let qi>0q_{i}>0, ∑iqi<∞\sum_{i}q_{i}<\infty, and let μ\mu, Φμ\Phi_{\mu}, and τB\tau_{B} be defined above. Then

Dq​(B)\displaystyle D_{q}(B) :=infbi≥0∑ibi≤B∑iqi​2−2​bi=Φμ​(τB).\displaystyle:=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{i}\geq 0\\ \sum_{i}b_{i}\leq B\end{subarray}}\sum_{i}q_{i}2^{-2b_{i}}=\Phi_{\mu}(\tau_{B}). (C.2)

For the bounded-logit value experiment,

ℜ∗value(n,B)≍RΦμ(n−1)+Φμ(τB).\boxed{\mathfrak{R}^{*}_{\rm value}(n,B)\asymp_{R}\Phi_{\mu}(n^{-1})+\Phi_{\mu}(\tau_{B}).} (C.3)

Moreover, for every t>0t>0,

Φμ,+′​(t)=μ⁡((t,∞)),Φμ,−′​(t)=μ⁡([t,∞)).\Phi^{\prime}_{\mu,+}(t)=\mu((t,\infty)),\qquad\Phi^{\prime}_{\mu,-}(t)=\mu([t,\infty)). (C.4)

Hence the exact curve Φμ\Phi_{\mu} recovers the positive spectrum, including atom multiplicities, up to coordinate relabeling.

Proof.

Summability gives 𝒩μ​(t)<∞\mathcal{N}_{\mu}(t)<\infty for every t>0t>0, and the largest positive energy is attained. Tonelli’s theorem yields

Φμ(t)=∑i∫0t𝟏{s<qi}ds=∑imin{qi,t},\Phi_{\mu}(t)=\sum_{i}\int_{0}^{t}\mathbf{1}\{s<q_{i}\}\,\mathrm{d}s=\sum_{i}\min\{q_{i},t\},

which proves Equation 3.1. For a finite storage budget, reverse water filling has rates

bi∗=12​log2​(qi/τB)+.b_{i}^{*}=\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}(q_{i}/\tau_{B})_{+}.

Here the positive part applies to the logarithm. To justify the optimizer without interchanging a limit and an infimum, write

On every compact subinterval of (0,qmax](0,q_{\max}], only finitely many summands can be nonzero. This proves existence and uniqueness of τB\tau_{B} for B>0B>0; for B=0B=0 take τ0=qmax\tau_{0}=q_{\max}. For λ=2​(ln⁡2)​τB\lambda=2(\ln 2)\tau_{B}, scalar convexity gives, for every bi≥0b_{i}\geq 0,

qi​2−2​bi+λ​bi≥qi​2−2​bi∗+λ​bi∗.q_{i}2^{-2b_{i}}+\lambda b_{i}\geq q_{i}2^{-2b_{i}^{*}}+\lambda b_{i}^{*}.

All distortion sums are bounded by ∑iqi\sum_{i}q_{i}, and the two bit sums are finite. This proves optimality directly in the countable problem. Since qi​2−2​bi∗=min⁡{qi,τB}q_{i}2^{-2b_{i}^{*}}=\min\{q_{i},\tau_{B}\}, this proves Equation 3.2. The bounded-logit curvature, Assouad, and arbitrary codebook bounds, proved in Theorem G.2, give ℜvalue∗(n,B)≍R𝒮q(n)+Dq(B)\mathfrak{R}^{*}_{\rm value}(n,B)\asymp_{R}\mathcal{S}_{q}(n)+D_{q}(B), proving Equation 3.3. Finally, for 0<h<t/20<h<t/2, both one-sided difference quotients of min⁡{qi,t}\min\{q_{i},t\} lie in [0,1][0,1] and vanish whenever qi<t/2q_{i}<t/2. There are only finitely many remaining coordinates. Taking their limits gives respectively 𝟏{qi>t}\mathbf{1}\{q_{i}>t\} and 𝟏{qi≥t}\mathbf{1}\{q_{i}\geq t\}, proving Equation 3.4. Proposition C.3 (Exact query–key realization; formal version of Proposition 4.1).

Under the strict causal mask exposing exactly the KK preceding candidates, Equation 4.1 reproduces the route-table scores and attention probabilities exactly. If only the query-address block of WQW_{Q} is trained and WKW_{K} is fixed, Euclidean SGD on WQW_{Q} induces the same update of AA; the attended feature and output-vector gradient are unchanged.

Proof.

Because PQ​xq=eqP_{Q}x_{q}=e_{q}, PC​xs=esP_{C}x_{s}=e_{s}, and J⊤​J=IKJ^{\top}J=I_{K}, direct substitution gives Equation 4.1. If G=∇AℓG=\nabla_{A}\ell, the physical query-projection gradient is ∇WQℓ=J​G⊤​PQ\nabla_{W_{Q}}\ell=JG^{\top}P_{Q}. Restricting training to this address block therefore maps one Euclidean step to WQ​(A−η​G)W_{Q}(A-\eta G). The scores, candidate-only masked softmax, and attended value feature coincide. The output loss sees the same feature, so its gradient with respect to ww also coincides. Orthogonality of the residual subspace to ww makes the residual logit zero. ∎

Theorem C.5 (Causal self-attention realization; formal version of Theorem 4.3).

For the source in Section 3, let Stage A start from zero and use the routing update in Proposition 4.2 on SAS_{A} independent calibration blocks. Freeze the route before Stage V, which uses n≥1n\geq 1 independent labeled blocks. With public pi,Δip_{i},\Delta_{i}, set

Theorem C.6 (Same block marginals, different scaling laws; formal version of Theorem 3.3).

For every χ,γ>0\chi,\gamma>0, there are two positive-conditional-entropy causal-retrieval sources with exactly the same block-energy multiset and the same block-dimension multiset at every dyadic level. They differ only in the pairing. All displayed dimensions in this construction are rounded upward to integers. With the common fixed-KK route revealed,

ℜeasy(n,B)≍n−χ/(1+χ)+B−χ,\mathfrak{R}_{\rm easy}(n,B)\asymp n^{-\chi/(1+\chi)}+B^{-\chi},

whereas

ℜhard(n,B)≍n−χ/(1+χ+γ)+B−χ/(1+γ).\mathfrak{R}_{\rm hard}(n,B)\asymp n^{-\chi/(1+\chi+\gamma)}+B^{-\chi/(1+\gamma)}.
Proof.

Fix δ>γ​χ\delta>\gamma\chi. At each level ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, take 2ℓ2^{\ell} blocks of energy c​2−(1+χ)​ℓc2^{-(1+\chi)\ell} and 2ℓ2^{\ell} blocks of energy c​2−(1+χ+δ)​ℓc2^{-(1+\chi+\delta)\ell}. The dimension multiset consists of 2ℓ2^{\ell} copies each of 11 and dℓ=⌈2γ​ℓ⌉d_{\ell}=\lceil 2^{\gamma\ell}\rceil. In the easy pairing the higher energy has dimension one; in the hard pairing it has dimension dℓd_{\ell}. Divide a block’s energy equally among its coordinates. Both multisets agree exactly at every level, including after the integer rounding of dimensions.

To realize these spectra as sources, choose any fixed radius R0>0R_{0}>0 within the logit bound, and choose c>0c>0 so that total energy is R02R_{0}^{2}. Give a coordinate of energy qiq_{i} probability pi=qi/R02p_{i}=q_{i}/R_{0}^{2} and radius Δi=R0\Delta_{i}=R_{0}. These probabilities sum to one. Independent candidate draws and the same fixed-KK retrieval map give the source in Section 3; bounded Bernoulli logits give strictly positive conditional entropy.

A generic component with exponent s>0s>0 and dimension exponent g≥0g\geq 0 has Θ⁡(2(1+g)​ℓ)\Theta(2^{(1+g)\ell}) coordinates of energy Θ⁡(2−(1+s+g)​ℓ)\Theta(2^{-(1+s+g)\ell}) at level ℓ\ell. The active levels at threshold tt lie between two cutoffs differing by a constant number of levels, each of size log2⁡(1/t)/(1+s+g)\log_{2}(1/t)/(1+s+g). A geometric sum therefore gives

Ns,g​(t)≍t−ρ⁡(s,g),ρ⁡(s,g)=1+g1+s+g.N_{s,g}(t)\asymp t^{-\rho(s,g)},\qquad\rho(s,g)=\frac{1+g}{1+s+g}.

Use the two-sided integral comparison at the end of the preceding spectral proof, rather than regular variation: dyadic spectra can have log-periodic fluctuations. This gives data and storage exponents s/(1+s+g)s/(1+s+g) and s/(1+g)s/(1+g), respectively. The easy components have (s,g)=(χ,0),(χ+δ,γ)(s,g)=(\chi,0),(\chi+\delta,\gamma). The inequality δ>γ​χ\delta>\gamma\chi makes the second component’s two exponents strictly larger. The hard components have (s,g)=(χ,γ),(χ+δ,0)(s,g)=(\chi,\gamma),(\chi+\delta,0), again with the second faster. For data, component errors add exactly. For storage, each full distortion is at least that of the slower component at budget BB, while allocating B/2B/2 to each component gives the matching upper bound. Applying Theorem C.1 now proves all four displayed rates. ∎

Appendix D Preliminaries and Notation

We begin by specifying what is observed, what is predicted, and which resources are counted. Section D.1 introduces the regenerative autoregressive source. Section D.2 defines held-out loss and learners with finitely many data-dependent states. Section D.3 adds mode-dependent representation costs, and Section D.4 distinguishes learned bits from physical storage and arithmetic cost.

D.1 A regenerative autoregressive source

This section writes the revealed-coordinate value problem with scalar index jj: Δj\Delta_{j} is the logit radius denoted RiR_{i} in the main text, and 𝔈∗​(n,B)\mathfrak{E}^{*}(n,B) below is ℜvalue∗​(n,B)\mathfrak{R}^{*}_{\rm value}(n,B). For a positive integer mm, write [m]={1,…,m}[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}, and let ℕ0={0,1,2,…}\mathbb{N}_{0}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}. We write Ber⁡(p)\Ber(p) for the Bernoulli distribution with success probability pp.

One regeneration block contains KK candidate tokens followed by a query and a binary target token. Candidate t∈[K]t\in[K] carries a public address ata_{t} and an observed mode label jtj_{t}. The query carries one address at⋆a_{t_{\star}}, so its causally relevant mode is

J≔jt⋆,ℙ⁡(J=j)=pj.J\coloneqq j_{t_{\star}},\qquad\mathbb{P}(J=j)=p_{j}.

Conditionally on J=jJ=j, the next token obeys

Y∣J=j∼Ber(σ(θj)),σ(z)=11+e−z.Y\mid J=j\sim\Ber(\sigma(\theta_{j})),\qquad\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}.

The parameter is θ=(θj)j≥1\theta=(\theta_{j})_{j\geq 1} with θj∈[−Δj,Δj]⊆[−R,R]\theta_{j}\in[-\Delta_{j},\Delta_{j}]\subseteq[-R,R], where R<∞R<\infty is fixed. We define the predictive energy

qj≔pj​Δj2q_{j}\coloneqq p_{j}\Delta_{j}^{2}

and assume ∑jqj<∞\sum_{j}q_{j}<\infty. We write Z=({(at,jt)}t=1K,at⋆,Y)∈𝒵Z=(\{(a_{t},j_{t})\}_{t=1}^{K},a_{t_{\star}},Y)\in\mathcal{Z} for the observed training block; the source parameters (θj)j(\theta_{j})_{j} are unknown. A regeneration delimiter resets the random variables, making distinct blocks independent. Tokens inside a block are causally ordered, but the statistical sample size nn counts independent blocks, not tokens. Bounded logits imply 0<σ⁡(−R)≤ℙ⁡(Y=1∣J)≤σ⁡(R)<10<\sigma(-R)\leq\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid J)\leq\sigma(R)<1, so the conditional entropy and Bayes cross-entropy are strictly positive.

D.2 Held-out risk and finite learned states

For a logit predictor f=(fj)jf=(f_{j})_{j}, define held-out cross-entropy

ℒθ​(f)≔𝔼θ​[−Y​log⁡σ⁡(fJ)−(1−Y)​log⁡(1−σ⁡(fJ))].\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(f)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\!\left[-Y\log\sigma(f_{J})-(1-Y)\log(1-\sigma(f_{J}))\right].

The Bayes predictor is fj=θjf_{j}=\theta_{j}; its loss is denoted ℒ∞≔ℒθ​(θ)>0\mathcal{L}_{\infty}\coloneqq\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(\theta)>0. Training and evaluation regeneration blocks are independent.

For an integer B≥0B\geq 0, a BB-bit learner consists of an encoder

ϕ:𝒵n⟶[2B]\phi:\mathcal{Z}^{n}\longrightarrow[2^{B}]

and a fixed decoder g:[2B]×ℕ→[−R,R]g:[2^{B}]\times\mathbb{N}\to[-R,R]. The decoder may share arbitrary computation across modes; only its data-dependent state is limited to 2B2^{B} possibilities. Randomized learners are allowed, although conditioning on their random seed shows that they do not improve the Bayes lower bounds used below. Because the Bayes loss depends on θ\theta, we define minimax excess risk directly and use the notation

𝔈∗​(n,B)≔infϕ,gsupθj∈[−Δj,Δj]𝔼θ​[ℒθ​(g⁡(ϕ⁡(Zn),⋅))−ℒθ​(θ)].\mathfrak{E}^{*}(n,B)\coloneqq\inf_{\phi,g}\sup_{\theta_{j}\in[-\Delta_{j},\Delta_{j}]}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(g(\phi(Z^{n}),\cdot))-\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(\theta)\right].

We use x≍yx\asymp y when positive constants bound their ratio in both directions. These constants may depend on RR and on stated regular-variation constants, but not on nn, BB, or the number of active modes.
