The statistical theorem uses qjq_{j}. The structural theorem allows a more general representable energy aj>0a_{j}>0, a per-bit difficulty cj>0c_{j}>0, and a numerical amplification κj>0\kappa_{j}>0. Assigning bj≥0b_{j}\geq 0 bits to mode jj incurs distortion aj​2−2​bja_{j}2^{-2b_{j}} and cost cj​bjc_{j}b_{j}. Its optimal distortion under budget BB is

D⁡(B)≔infbj≥0∑jcj​bj≤B∑jaj​2−2​bj.D(B)\coloneqq\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{j}\geq 0\\ \sum_{j}c_{j}b_{j}\leq B\end{subarray}}\sum_{j}a_{j}2^{-2b_{j}}. (D.1)

Let vj≥0v_{j}\geq 0 record a separately specified statistical residual for mode jj. This auxiliary quantity is used in the complete tuple summary below, not in the spectral formula for D⁡(B)D(B). For a finite mode collection, the unlabeled joint measure

η≔∑jδ(vj,aj,cj,κj)\eta\coloneqq\sum_{j}\delta_{(v_{j},a_{j},c_{j},\kappa_{j})} (D.2)

records statistical residual vjv_{j}, representable energy, difficulty, and amplification together. The cost-weighted difficulty-normalized spectrum is

μ≔∑jcj​δaj/cj.\mu\coloneqq\sum_{j}c_{j}\,\delta_{a_{j}/c_{j}}. (D.3)

For unit costs and aj=qja_{j}=q_{j}, this reduces to the coordinate spectrum in Section 3; general costs weight each atom by cjc_{j}. We will compare unlabeled summaries of these mode-dependent quantities. Such a summary is sufficient for the complete budget–distortion curve if equal summary values imply equal D⁡(B)D(B) for every B≥0B\geq 0.

D.4 Neural and arithmetic resources

In Section 5, X∈ℝ(K+1)×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{(K+1)\times d} denotes the matrix of candidate and query token vectors, and U∈ℝd×dU\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} denotes the bilinear attention score matrix. The symbol NN counts physically stored dense scalar parameter slots. It is not identified with BB, the number of bits in the data-dependent learned state.

The symbol CC denotes a non-statistical cost budget: representation cost in Appendix F and arithmetic computation in Sections B.3 and 6. These meanings occur in separate results and are never equated. When CC denotes computation, its arithmetic cost model is stated explicitly. In Section 6, one bb-bit scalar operation costs Θ⁡(bν)\Theta(b^{\nu}), where ν≥0\nu\geq 0 is fixed. In Section B.3, ℓ\ell, dd, mffm_{\rm ff}, HH, and LL denote sequence length, hidden width, feed-forward width, attention-head count, and layer count. The symbol bmmb_{\rm mm} indexes a matrix-arithmetic format family whose operand, output, and accumulator widths are prescribed functions of bmmb_{\rm mm}; bsmb_{\rm sm} specifies the effective softmax precision; and bstb_{\rm st} is the number of bits used to store an attention probability. Unit roundoff is denoted uu. These variables specify arithmetic work and storage; Appendix A discusses their relation to implementations.

Appendix E Learning after Data: A Finite-Bit Autoregressive Minimax Law

Two irreducible losses govern finite-bit prediction. We first lower-bound the distortion of any learned state with at most 2B2^{B} possible values, even when its coordinates are decoded jointly. We then combine this bound with statistical uncertainty across regeneration blocks and evaluate the resulting risk law for power-law energies. Full proofs appear in Appendix G.

Lemma E.1 (Arbitrary joint finite-state representations; informal version of Lemma G.1).

Let Θj\Theta_{j} be independent and uniform on [−Δj,Δj][-\Delta_{j},\Delta_{j}], let pj>0p_{j}>0, and put qj=pj​Δj2q_{j}=p_{j}\Delta_{j}^{2}. For B∈ℕ0B\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, every encoder–decoder pair with at most 2B2^{B} reconstruction vectors satisfies

∑jpj​𝔼​(Θj−Θ^j)2≥2π​e​infbj≥0∑jbj≤B∑jqj​2−2​bj.\sum_{j}p_{j}\mathbb{E}(\Theta_{j}-\widehat{\Theta}_{j})^{2}\geq\frac{2}{\pi e}\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{j}\geq 0\\ \sum_{j}b_{j}\leq B\end{subarray}}\sum_{j}q_{j}2^{-2b_{j}}. (E.1)

The reconstruction vectors may couple all coordinates.

Here the codebook is simply the set of at most 2B2^{B} reconstruction vectors available to the decoder. The entropy proof controls total codebook cardinality, so it covers shared representations that compress several modes jointly as well as coordinatewise quantizers.

Theorem E.2 (Finite-bit autoregressive minimax law; informal version of Theorem G.2).

Fix R<∞R<\infty. For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, B∈ℕ0B\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, and source family specified by (pj,Δj)j≥1(p_{j},\Delta_{j})_{j\geq 1} as in Section D.1, there are constants 0<cR≤CR<∞0<c_{R}\leq C_{R}<\infty such that

cR​{Sq​(n)+Dq​(B)}≤𝔈∗​(n,B)≤CR​{Sq​(n)+Dq​(B)},c_{R}\{S_{q}(n)+D_{q}(B)\}\leq\mathfrak{E}^{*}(n,B)\leq C_{R}\{S_{q}(n)+D_{q}(B)\}, (E.2)

where

Sq​(n)≔∑jmin⁡{qj,n−1},Dq​(B)≔infbj≥0∑jbj≤B∑jqj​2−2​bj.S_{q}(n)\coloneqq\sum_{j}\min\{q_{j},n^{-1}\},\qquad D_{q}(B)\coloneqq\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{j}\geq 0\\ \sum_{j}b_{j}\leq B\end{subarray}}\sum_{j}q_{j}2^{-2b_{j}}. (E.3)

The lower bound holds for arbitrary 2B2^{B}-state joint encoders and arbitrary fixed shared decoding computation.

Why the two terms add.

On bounded logits, excess Bernoulli cross-entropy is equivalent to squared logit error. A clipped modewise likelihood estimate contributes min⁡{qj,1/n}\min\{q_{j},1/n\}: a rare or weak mode is no harder to ignore than to estimate. Quantizing the resulting coordinates according to a feasible (bj)(b_{j}) contributes qj​2−2​bjq_{j}2^{-2b_{j}}. For the converse, an Assouad hypercube gives the statistical term. Giving the encoder the true parameter can only make representation easier; Lemma E.1 then gives the bit term. The actual risk exceeds the maximum of these two lower bounds, which is at least half their sum. This proves the constant-factor equivalence in Equation E.2.

Corollary E.3 (Power-law energies; informal version of Corollary G.3).

Suppose that n,B≥1n,B\geq 1 and, for some χ>0\chi>0 and constants 0<c−≤c+<∞0<c_{-}\leq c_{+}<\infty,

c−​j−(1+χ)≤qj≤c+​j−(1+χ)(j≥1).c_{-}j^{-(1+\chi)}\leq q_{j}\leq c_{+}j^{-(1+\chi)}\qquad(j\geq 1).

Then

𝔈∗(n,B)≍n−χ/(1+χ)+B−χ.\mathfrak{E}^{*}(n,B)\asymp n^{-\chi/(1+\chi)}+B^{-\chi}. (E.4)

The data–bit crossover occurs at B≍n1/(1+χ)B\asymp n^{1/(1+\chi)}.

To see the two exponents, split Sq​(n)S_{q}(n) where qjq_{j} crosses 1/n1/n. For Dq​(B)D_{q}(B), reverse water filling equalizes qj​2−2​bjq_{j}2^{-2b_{j}} on active modes. If mm modes are active, Stirling’s formula gives B≍mB\asymp m, while active distortion and the inactive tail are both ≍m−χ\asymp m^{-\chi}.

What the law identifies.

The theorem identifies the data and retained-bit dependence for the stated positive-entropy autoregressive source. Its distinctive role is to couple held-out log-loss with arbitrary shared decoding; the next structural results show what additional information determines the resulting exponent.

Appendix F Why Marginal Summaries Do Not Determine Scaling

This section asks which information about mode difficulty identifies a scaling law. Here cost is charged directly to selecting or representing a coordinate. The main-text construction instead realizes difficulty through the number of independent coordinates within an energy group. Two problems with identical energy and cost marginals first show what separate summaries lose. The joint spectrum then recovers exactly the complete budget–distortion curve and gives the smallest exact summary for separable allocation.

F.1 Same marginals, different exponents

Consider first a binary selection rule. Selecting mode jj pays cjc_{j} and removes energy qjq_{j}; unselected energy remains as error. Under total representation-cost budget CC, its optimum is

𝒜⁡(C)≔infS⊆ℕ∑j∈Scj≤C∑j∉Sqj.\mathcal{A}(C)\coloneqq\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq\mathbb{N}\\ \sum_{j\in S}c_{j}\leq C\end{subarray}}\sum_{j\notin S}q_{j}. (F.1)
Theorem F.1 (Marginals do not identify scaling; informal version of Theorem I.1).

For every χ,γ>0\chi,\gamma>0, there are two instances of Equation F.1 with identical energy multisets and identical cost multisets at every dyadic level, but

𝒜easy(C)≍C−χ,𝒜hard(C)≍C−χ/(1+γ).\mathcal{A}_{\rm easy}(C)\asymp C^{-\chi},\qquad\mathcal{A}_{\rm hard}(C)\asymp C^{-\chi/(1+\gamma)}. (F.2)

The same two exponents hold when selection is replaced by continuous bits with distortion qj​2−2​bjq_{j}2^{-2b_{j}} and cost cj​bjc_{j}b_{j}. Hence no summary that retains only the two marginal multisets identifies the optimal exponent in either representation class.

The construction makes the missing information visible. At level ℓ\ell, create 2ℓ2^{\ell} high-energy modes of size 2−(1+χ)​ℓ2^{-(1+\chi)\ell} and 2ℓ2^{\ell} lower-energy modes of size 2−(1+χ+δ)​ℓ2^{-(1+\chi+\delta)\ell}, with δ>γ​χ\delta>\gamma\chi. The costs are 2ℓ2^{\ell} copies of 11 and 2ℓ2^{\ell} copies of 2γ​ℓ2^{\gamma\ell}. The easy instance pairs high energy with unit cost; the hard instance pairs it with the larger cost. All marginals agree level by level. A component with multiplicity 2ℓ2^{\ell}, energy 2−(1+s)​ℓ2^{-(1+s)\ell}, and cost 2g​ℓ2^{g\ell} has exponent s/(1+g)s/(1+g). This yields Equation F.2; the full lower bound also permits non-prefix selections through a fractional relaxation.

The causal-source coupling experiment is shown in Figure 3(b,e), together with analytic distortion; Table 2(b) compares theoretical and held-out slopes.

F.2 The joint spectrum

The full unlabeled joint measure η\eta in Equation D.2 retains the pairing by construction. For the separable exponential response Equation D.1, it can be compressed further.

Theorem F.2 (Joint energy–difficulty characterization; informal version of Theorem I.2).

For a finite collection of modes, η\eta is a maximal invariant under permutations of mode labels: it retains all information except the arbitrary names of the modes. For a finite or countable collection, consider the separable problem Equation D.1 and assume

∑jaj<∞,∑j:aj/cj>tcj<∞for every t>0.\sum_{j}a_{j}<\infty,\qquad\sum_{j:a_{j}/c_{j}>t}c_{j}<\infty\quad\text{for every }t>0.

Then the spectrum μ=∑jcj​δaj/cj\mu=\sum_{j}c_{j}\delta_{a_{j}/c_{j}} determines D⁡(B)D(B) for every B≥0B\geq 0. Conversely, the complete curve B↦D⁡(B)B\mapsto D(B) determines μ\mu on (0,∞)(0,\infty). Consequently, μ\mu is a minimal exact unlabeled summary of the complete budget–distortion curve for this representation class.

Put rj=aj/cjr_{j}=a_{j}/c_{j}. The coordinatewise optimum has a water level τ>0\tau>0:

bj​(τ)=12​log2​(rj/τ)+.b_{j}(\tau)=\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}(r_{j}/\tau)_{+}. (F.3)

Writing the result in terms of μ\mu gives two integral identities,

B⁡(τ)=12​log⁡2​∫log⁡(r/τ)+​μ​(𝑑r),D⁡(B⁡(τ))=∫min⁡{r,τ}​μ​(𝑑r).B(\tau)=\frac{1}{2\log 2}\int\log(r/\tau)_{+}\,\mu(\,\mathrm{d}r),\qquad D(B(\tau))=\int\min\{r,\tau\}\,\mu(\,\mathrm{d}r). (F.4)

These identities prove sufficiency. They also make the inverse result possible. At differentiability points the envelope theorem gives

D′​(B)=−2​log⁡2​τ​(B).D^{\prime}(B)=-2\log 2\,\tau(B). (F.5)

Thus the curve recovers the water level, hence B⁡(τ)B(\tau). With s=log⁡τs=\log\tau,

dd​s​B​(es)=−12​log⁡2​μ​((es,∞))\frac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}s}B(e^{s})=-\frac{1}{2\log 2}\mu((e^{s},\infty)) (F.6)

at every continuity point. The right-continuous tail, including its jumps, determines μ\mu.

Minimality now has a precise meaning. If another summary TT determines the complete curve, then T⁡(x)=T⁡(y)T(x)=T(y) implies Dx=DyD_{x}=D_{y}, which by Equation F.6 implies μx=μy\mu_{x}=\mu_{y}. Therefore μ\mu is a function of every sufficient summary. It is also strictly coarser than the full unlabeled table η\eta: it retains only the cost-weighted distribution of energy per unit difficulty.

Corollary F.3 (Joint-tail exponent).

If aj≍j−αa_{j}\asymp j^{-\alpha} with α>1\alpha>1 and cj≍jγc_{j}\asymp j^{\gamma} with γ>−1\gamma>-1, then

D(B)≍B−(α−1)/(1+γ).D(B)\asymp B^{-(\alpha-1)/(1+\gamma)}.

Indeed, the active threshold mm obeys B≍m1+γB\asymp m^{1+\gamma}, while the represented distortion and omitted tail are both ≍m1−α\asymp m^{1-\alpha}.

When the ingredients can be measured.

Controlled interventions provide a route to estimating the ingredients: counts estimate mode frequency, held-out ablations estimate predictive energy, and deliberate rounding perturbations estimate numerical amplification. The identification theorem specifies how these quantities determine the resource curve; extracting them from passive natural-language observations is an open estimation problem.

Appendix G Proofs for the Finite-Bit Autoregressive Minimax Law

This appendix proves the arbitrary-codebook entropy lemma, the statistical upper and lower bounds, and the power-law corollary in that order.

Lemma G.1 (Arbitrary joint finite-state representations; formal version of Lemma E.1).

Theorem G.2 (Finite-bit autoregressive minimax law; formal version of Theorem E.2).

Fix R<∞R<\infty. For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, B∈ℕ0B\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, and source family specified by (pj,Δj)j≥1(p_{j},\Delta_{j})_{j\geq 1} as in Section D.1, there are constants 0<cR≤CR<∞0<c_{R}\leq C_{R}<\infty such that

cR​{Sq​(n)+Dq​(B)}≤𝔈∗​(n,B)≤CR​{Sq​(n)+Dq​(B)},c_{R}\{S_{q}(n)+D_{q}(B)\}\leq\mathfrak{E}^{*}(n,B)\leq C_{R}\{S_{q}(n)+D_{q}(B)\}, (G.4)

where

Sq​(n)≔∑jmin⁡{qj,n−1},Dq​(B)≔infbj≥0∑jbj≤B∑jqj​2−2​bj.S_{q}(n)\coloneqq\sum_{j}\min\{q_{j},n^{-1}\},\qquad D_{q}(B)\coloneqq\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}b_{j}\geq 0\\ \sum_{j}b_{j}\leq B\end{subarray}}\sum_{j}q_{j}2^{-2b_{j}}. (G.5)

The lower bound holds for arbitrary 2B2^{B}-state joint encoders and arbitrary fixed shared decoding computation.

Proof.

We proceed in four steps.

Step 1: loss curvature.

The Bernoulli log-partition function A⁡(t)=log⁡(1+et)A(t)=\log(1+e^{t}) satisfies

On [−R,R][-R,R], this derivative lies between two positive constants. The excess cross-entropy of logit θ^\widehat{\theta} is the Bregman divergence of AA, or equivalently the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, which we denote by KL\KL. Taylor’s theorem therefore yields

cR(θ−θ^)2≤KL(Ber(σ(θ))∥Ber(σ(θ^)))≤CR(θ−θ^)2.c_{R}(\theta-\widehat{\theta})^{2}\leq\KL(\Ber(\sigma(\theta))\,\|\,\Ber(\sigma(\widehat{\theta})))\leq C_{R}(\theta-\widehat{\theta})^{2}. (G.6)

Clipping a decoded logit to [−R,R][-R,R] also cannot increase cross-entropy: the derivative with respect to the decoded logit zz is σ⁡(z)−σ⁡(θ)\sigma(z)-\sigma(\theta), which has the sign of z−θz-\theta. Clipping preserves the decoder’s cardinality. Thus both minimax bounds can be proved using bounded decoded logits and weighted squared error.

Step 2: statistical upper bound.

Let Nj∼Binomial⁡(n,pj)N_{j}\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p_{j}) be the training count of mode jj. If Nj≥1N_{j}\geq 1, project the empirical Bernoulli mean onto [σ⁡(−Δj),σ⁡(Δj)][\sigma(-\Delta_{j}),\sigma(\Delta_{j})] and apply the logit map. Projection cannot increase probability error, and the logit is Lipschitz on [σ⁡(−R),σ⁡(R)][\sigma(-R),\sigma(R)]. Thus its conditional mean-square error is at most CR/NjC_{R}/N_{j}. The zero estimator has error at most Δj2\Delta_{j}^{2}. Choose between them using the observed count, yielding

𝔼⁡[(θ^j−θj)2∣Nj]≤CR′​min⁡{Δj2,(Nj+1)−1}.\mathbb{E}[(\widehat{\theta}_{j}-\theta_{j})^{2}\mid N_{j}]\leq C_{R}^{\prime}\min\{\Delta_{j}^{2},(N_{j}+1)^{-1}\}. (G.7)

The identity

𝔼​1Nj+1=1−(1−pj)n+1(n+1)​pj≤1(n+1)​pj\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{N_{j}+1}=\frac{1-(1-p_{j})^{n+1}}{(n+1)p_{j}}\leq\frac{1}{(n+1)p_{j}} (G.8)

follows by integrating the binomial generating function. Therefore

pj​𝔼​(θ^j−θj)2\displaystyle p_{j}\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\theta}_{j}-\theta_{j})^{2} ≤CR′​min⁡{pj​Δj2,pj​𝔼​1Nj+1}\displaystyle\leq C_{R}^{\prime}\min\left\{p_{j}\Delta_{j}^{2},\,p_{j}\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{N_{j}+1}\right\}
≤CR′′​min⁡{qj,n−1}.\displaystyle\leq C_{R}^{\prime\prime}\min\{q_{j},n^{-1}\}.

Summing proves the Sq​(n)S_{q}(n) upper bound.

Now select an allocation within an arbitrarily small additive error of Dq​(B)D_{q}(B), round each positive bjb_{j} down to an integer, and uniformly quantize the clipped estimate on [−Δj,Δj][-\Delta_{j},\Delta_{j}]. Flooring uses at most BB bits and enlarges 2−2​bj2^{-2b_{j}} by at most four. By the squared triangle inequality and Equation G.6,

𝔈∗​(n,B)≤CR​{Sq​(n)+Dq​(B)}.\mathfrak{E}^{*}(n,B)\leq C_{R}\{S_{q}(n)+D_{q}(B)\}. (G.9)

Fix a finite coordinate set AA. On coordinate j∈Aj\in A, use the two parameters ±δj\pm\delta_{j}, where

δj=cR′min{Δj,(npj)−1/2}\delta_{j}=c_{R}^{\prime}\min\{\Delta_{j},(np_{j})^{-1/2}\}

and cR′>0c_{R}^{\prime}>0 is sufficiently small. Neighboring hypercube vertices differ only when J=jJ=j, and bounded Bernoulli curvature gives

Give the encoder θ\theta in addition to the data. This enlarges the encoder class and can only reduce its minimax risk. Under the product-uniform prior on the parameter box, Lemma E.1 gives

Corollary G.3 (Power-law energies; formal version of Corollary E.3).

Suppose that n,B≥1n,B\geq 1 and, for some χ>0\chi>0 and constants 0<c−≤c+<∞0<c_{-}\leq c_{+}<\infty,

c−​j−(1+χ)≤qj≤c+​j−(1+χ)(j≥1).c_{-}j^{-(1+\chi)}\leq q_{j}\leq c_{+}j^{-(1+\chi)}\qquad(j\geq 1).

Appendix H Proof of Adaptation with a Known Ordering

This appendix verifies that one rounded schedule works uniformly over the specified exponent interval.

Theorem H.1 (Adaptation with a known ordering; formal version of Theorem 5.1).

Fix 0<χmin≤χmax<∞0<\chi_{\min}\leq\chi_{\max}<\infty, and suppose the canonical mode order is known. Assume qj≍j−(1+χ)q_{j}\asymp j^{-(1+\chi)} with common comparison constants and unknown χ∈[χmin,χmax]\chi\in[\chi_{\min},\chi_{\max}]. For every n,B∈ℕn,B\in\mathbb{N}, one clipped likelihood estimator and one deterministic integer bit schedule, both independent of χ\chi, satisfy simultaneously throughout this interval

supθj∈[−Δj,Δj]𝔼θ[ℒθ(f^)−ℒθ(θ)]≲n−χ/(1+χ)+B−χ.\sup_{\theta_{j}\in[-\Delta_{j},\Delta_{j}]}\mathbb{E}_{\theta}\!\left[\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(\widehat{f})-\mathcal{L}_{\theta}(\theta)\right]\lesssim n^{-\chi/(1+\chi)}+B^{-\chi}. (H.1)

The estimator in the statistical upper bound of Theorem E.2 uses only NjN_{j}, Δj\Delta_{j}, and the observed labels, not χ\chi. It contributes Sq(n)≍n−χ/(1+χ)S_{q}(n)\asymp n^{-\chi/(1+\chi)}.

Choose A>χmax/2A>\chi_{\max}/2. Before rounding, the schedule in Equation 5.2 uses

A​∑j≤mlog2⁡(m/j)=A​log2⁡(mm/m!)=Θ⁡(m).A\sum_{j\leq m}\log_{2}(m/j)=A\log_{2}(m^{m}/m!)=\Theta(m).

Flooring enlarges each nonzero distortion by at most four. Consequently, uniformly over χ≤χmax\chi\leq\chi_{\max},

∑j≤mqj​2−2​bj\displaystyle\sum_{j\leq m}q_{j}2^{-2b_{j}} ≲m−2​A​∑j≤mj2​A−1−χ\displaystyle\lesssim m^{-2A}\sum_{j\leq m}j^{2A-1-\chi}
≲m−χ,\displaystyle\lesssim m^{-\chi},

Appendix I Proofs for Joint Difficulty

This appendix proves the same-marginal separation and then the positive joint-summary theorem.

Theorem I.1 (Marginals do not identify scaling; formal version of Theorem F.1).

For every χ,γ>0\chi,\gamma>0, there are two instances of Equation F.1 with identical energy multisets and identical cost multisets at every dyadic level, but

𝒜easy(C)≍C−χ,𝒜hard(C)≍C−χ/(1+γ).\mathcal{A}_{\rm easy}(C)\asymp C^{-\chi},\qquad\mathcal{A}_{\rm hard}(C)\asymp C^{-\chi/(1+\gamma)}. (I.1)

The same two exponents hold when selection is replaced by continuous bits with distortion qj​2−2​bjq_{j}2^{-2b_{j}} and cost cj​bjc_{j}b_{j}. Hence no summary that retains only the two marginal multisets identifies the optimal exponent in either representation class.

Proof.

Fix δ>γ​χ\delta>\gamma\chi. At each level ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1, create two groups, each of multiplicity 2ℓ2^{\ell}. Their energies are

qℓH=2−(1+χ)​ℓ,qℓL=2−(1+χ+δ)​ℓ,q_{\ell}^{\rm H}=2^{-(1+\chi)\ell},\qquad q_{\ell}^{\rm L}=2^{-(1+\chi+\delta)\ell},

and the level’s cost multiset contains 2ℓ2^{\ell} copies of 11 and 2ℓ2^{\ell} copies of 2γ​ℓ2^{\gamma\ell}. The easy instance pairs qℓHq_{\ell}^{\rm H} with unit cost; the hard instance pairs it with 2γ​ℓ2^{\gamma\ell}. The energy and cost multisets therefore agree at every level.

Consider a generic component of multiplicity 2ℓ2^{\ell}, per-item energy 2−(1+s)​ℓ2^{-(1+s)\ell}, and per-item cost 2g​ℓ2^{g\ell}. Buying the component through level LL costs

∑ℓ≤L2(1+g)​ℓ=Θ⁡(2(1+g)​L),\sum_{\ell\leq L}2^{(1+g)\ell}=\Theta(2^{(1+g)L}),

and leaves energy

∑ℓ>L2−s​ℓ=Θ⁡(2−s​L).\sum_{\ell>L}2^{-s\ell}=\Theta(2^{-sL}).

Thus its selection exponent is s/(1+g)s/(1+g). This prefix is also a matching lower bound: within the component, energy per cost decreases with ℓ\ell, so the fractional relaxation is a threshold policy, and every integral policy is no better.

In the easy instance, the high-energy component has exponent χ\chi, while the low-energy component has exponent (χ+δ)/(1+γ)>χ(\chi+\delta)/(1+\gamma)>\chi. Splitting the budget by fixed fractions therefore gives, and the high-energy relaxation lower-bounds, 𝒜easy​(C)≍C−χ\mathcal{A}_{\rm easy}(C)\asymp C^{-\chi}. In the hard instance, the high-energy component has exponent χ/(1+γ)\chi/(1+\gamma), while the low-energy unit-cost component has exponent χ+δ\chi+\delta. Hence 𝒜hard(C)≍C−χ/(1+γ)\mathcal{A}_{\rm hard}(C)\asymp C^{-\chi/(1+\gamma)}.

For continuous bits, the optimality condition on an active coordinate is

qj​2−2​bjcj=τ.\frac{q_{j}2^{-2b_{j}}}{c_{j}}=\tau.

For the generic component above, the active levels form a prefix through LL. At level ℓ\ell, bℓb_{\ell} is proportional to L−ℓL-\ell; therefore

∑ℓ≤L2(1+g)​ℓ​bℓ=Θ⁡(2(1+g)​L).\sum_{\ell\leq L}2^{(1+g)\ell}b_{\ell}=\Theta(2^{(1+g)L}).

Both active distortion and the inactive tail are Θ⁡(2−s​L)\Theta(2^{-sL}). The same exponent s/(1+g)s/(1+g) follows, and applying it to the four components completes the proof. ∎

Appendix K Proof of the Transformer Bit-Complexity Lemma

This appendix counts the dense forward–backward graph stated in Section B.3. Its sequence length, hidden width, feed-forward width, head count, and depth are ℓ,d,mff,H,L\ell,d,m_{\rm ff},H,L, respectively. The precision indices specify the operand, accumulator, and stored-activation formats whose costs are counted.

Lemma K.1 (Transformer forward–backward bit complexity; formal version of Lemma B.1).

For the graph above, with positive dimensions and conventional dense matrix multiplication,

BitOpsfb≍L⁡[(ℓ​d2+ℓ​d​mff+ℓ2​d)​𝖬​(bmm)+H​ℓ2​𝖲​(bsm)].\operatorname{BitOps}_{\rm fb}\asymp L\Bigl[\bigl(\ell d^{2}+\ell dm_{\rm ff}+\ell^{2}d\bigr)\mathsf{M}(b_{\rm mm})+H\ell^{2}\mathsf{S}(b_{\rm sm})\Bigr]. (K.1)
Memfb≍bw​L​(d2+d​mff)+ba​L​ℓ​(d+mff)+bst​L​H​ℓ2+Memhp.\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm fb}\asymp b_{w}L(d^{2}+dm_{\rm ff})+b_{a}L\ell(d+m_{\rm ff})+b_{\rm st}LH\ell^{2}+\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm hp}. (K.2)

The memory Memfb\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm fb} is measured in bits. The values bwb_{w}, bab_{a}, and bstb_{\rm st} count aggregate bits per logical weight, activation, and saved-attention slot at peak memory; they include any same-shaped gradient or backward-workspace buffer materialized by this eager implementation. The term Memhp\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm hp} contains master weights, optimizer state, and all other explicitly retained high-precision data. A streaming, recomputing attention implementation replaces the quadratic attention state saved for backward by linear online-softmax state plus temporary tile workspace, while leaving the dense attention arithmetic order unchanged.

Proof.

Suppressing constant head reshapes, the four query, key, value, and output projections perform 4​ℓ​d24\ell d^{2} multiply–accumulates per layer. Let QmatQ_{\rm mat}, KmatK_{\rm mat}, and VmatV_{\rm mat} denote the query, key, and value matrices, and let PP denote the matrix of attention probabilities. The query–key score product Qmat​Kmat⊤Q_{\rm mat}K_{\rm mat}^{\top} and probability–value product P​VmatPV_{\rm mat} each perform ℓ2​d\ell^{2}d, and the two feed-forward maps perform 2​ℓ​d​mff2\ell dm_{\rm ff}. Thus the forward matrix count is

Fmat=4​ℓ​d2+2​ℓ2​d+2​ℓ​d​mff.F_{\rm mat}=4\ell d^{2}+2\ell^{2}d+2\ell dm_{\rm ff}. (K.3)

For any product Y=A​BY=AB, reverse mode forms ∇A=∇YB⊤\nabla_{A}=\nabla_{Y}B^{\top} and ∇B=A⊤​∇Y\nabla_{B}=A^{\top}\nabla_{Y}. Each has the same scalar multiply–accumulate count as the forward product. Consequently the matrix part of one forward–backward pass is exactly three times Equation K.3, up to additions, transposes, and casts.

There are H​ℓH\ell softmax rows of length ℓ\ell. Stable max shifting, exponentiation, reduction, division, and the reverse-mode row calculation together cost Θ⁡(H​ℓ2​𝖲​(bsm))\Theta(H\ell^{2}\mathsf{S}(b_{\rm sm})) by the definition of 𝖲\mathsf{S}. Given an incoming row gradient vv, the softmax Jacobian is applied by

p⊙(v−⟨p,v⟩​𝟏),p\odot\bigl(v-\langle p,v\rangle\mathbf{1}\bigr),

which uses a constant number of length-ℓ\ell passes. No explicit ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell Jacobian is formed. Multiplying by LL and absorbing fixed projection constants proves Equation B.5. Normalization, pointwise activation, dropout, and casts have only O⁡(L​ℓ​(d+mff)+L​H​ℓ2)O(L\ell(d+m_{\rm ff})+LH\ell^{2}) scalar entries and are the stated lower-order terms for this computation.

For memory, the dense projection and feed-forward weights contain Θ⁡(L⁡(d2+d​mff))\Theta(L(d^{2}+dm_{\rm ff})) scalars. Saved residual, projection, and feed-forward activations contain Θ⁡(L​ℓ​(d+mff))\Theta(L\ell(d+m_{\rm ff})) scalars. Eager reverse mode also saves L​H​ℓ2LH\ell^{2} attention probabilities. Multiplying each collection by its aggregate bits per logical slot (including same-shaped peak gradient or workspace buffers) and adding separately retained high-precision state gives Equation B.6. A tiled online softmax stores row normalization statistics and tiles rather than the complete probability matrix, so its persistent attention state is linear in H​ℓH\ell; recomputing tiles during backward does not change the dense arithmetic order. These counts also give the two-sided bounds because each named tensor and matrix product is present in the specified graph. ∎

Appendix L Proof of the Compute–Precision Pareto Law

The proof distinguishes the precision required to match a target error from the exact precision chosen by a finite-budget optimizer.

Theorem L.1 (Compute–precision Pareto law; formal version of Theorem B.2).

Assume Equations B.7 and B.8, κmm​(M)≍Mr\kappa_{\rm mm}(M)\asymp M^{r}, and κsm​(M)≍Mrsm\kappa_{\rm sm}(M)\asymp M^{r_{\rm sm}}, with all displayed relations two-sided and r,rsm≥0r,r_{\rm sm}\geq 0. For the specified dense graph, H≤dH\leq d implies G≳SG\gtrsim S and hence g≥sg\geq s. Item 3 concerns general operation counts satisfying the same two-sided relations; items 1, 2, and 4 apply to both settings.

  1. 1.

    The smallest matrix precision that keeps matrix rounding at the model error is

    bmatch​(M)=(r+χ2)​log2​M+O⁡(1).b_{\rm match}(M)=\left(r+\frac{\chi}{2}\right)\log_{2}M+O(1). (L.1)
  2. 2.

    If the matrix term dominates the bracket in Equation B.8 at matched precisions—in particular in the case g≥sg\geq s when the remaining precision factors do not reverse that dominance—then

    infM,b,bsm:cost≤Cℰ≍C−χ/(1+χ+g)(logC)χ​ν/(1+χ+g),\inf_{M,b,b_{\rm sm}:\,\mathrm{cost}\leq C}\mathcal{E}\asymp C^{-\chi/(1+\chi+g)}(\log C)^{\chi\nu/(1+\chi+g)}, (L.2)

    up to other declared slowly varying factors.

    C1/(1+χ+s)≲22​bsm/(χ+2​rsm),C^{1/(1+\chi+s)}\lesssim 2^{2b_{\rm sm}/(\chi+2r_{\rm sm})},
    infM,b:cost≤Cℰ≍C−χ/(1+χ+s).\inf_{M,b:\,\mathrm{cost}\leq C}\mathcal{E}\asymp C^{-\chi/(1+\chi+s)}. (L.3)

    Reducing matrix precision cannot improve this leading exponent.

    At fixed matrix precision bb, with softmax precision optimized, the model–rounding crossover and the infimum error over model scales are

    Mb≍22​b/(χ+2​r),ℰfloor(b)≍2−2χb/(χ+2r).M_{b}\asymp 2^{2b/(\chi+2r)},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{\rm floor}(b)\asymp 2^{-2\chi b/(\chi+2r)}. (L.4)

    A fixed bsmb_{\rm sm}-bit softmax similarly supports the scaling phase only while

    M≲22​bsm/(χ+2​rsm).M\lesssim 2^{2b_{\rm sm}/(\chi+2r_{\rm sm})}. (L.5)

The displayed two-sided risk and arithmetic assumptions define the class over which the infima and matching bounds are taken.

The matrix rounding term is at most a constant multiple of the model term exactly when

M2​r​2−2​b≲M−χ.M^{2r}2^{-2b}\lesssim M^{-\chi}.

Appendix N Experimental Details

This appendix describes the 1,024-mode synthetic study. Its five-seed percentile intervals apply to this study; the other experiments use the BCa procedures and seed or item units specified in their respective captions.

Source families.

Each run uses 10241024 modes and bounded logits. For each χ∈{0.5,1,2}\chi\in\{0.5,1,2\}, two different frequency–amplitude decompositions produce the same power qj≍j−(1+χ)q_{j}\asymp j^{-(1+\chi)}. Training blocks are independent regenerations. Held-out cross-entropy is evaluated exactly from the population probabilities, so no test-set Monte Carlo error is mixed into the reported training-seed variability.

Grid and methods.

The grid contains four values of nn, five values of BB, three exponents, two decompositions, four allocation methods, and five seeds, for 4⋅5⋅3⋅2⋅4⋅5=24004\cdot 5\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 4\cdot 5=2400 configuration–seed pairs. The known-energy method solves the finite energy sequence’s water-filling problem. The universal method uses Equation 5.2. Uniform width assigns a common precision to a prefix, and shuffled allocation breaks the energy–precision pairing. Allocations never spend precision beyond the statistical resolution of a mode.

Uncertainty.

For each of the 480480 configurations, we report the mean over five seeds. The plotted interval is the 2.5 and 97.5 percentile envelope from 50005000 bootstrap resamples of the seed mean, using bootstrap seed zero and expanding the interval when necessary to contain the observed mean.

Reproducibility details.

The raw rows, summaries, deterministic analytic curves, plotting sources, and experiment code accompany the paper. The experiments use local CPUs, one common exponent specification across configurations, and analytic arithmetic cost as the theoretical resource.

Appendix O Mixed Precision in Practice

The resource variables in Section B.3 deliberately separate compute precision from storage precision. In the asymptotic Pareto theorem, bb is an effective accuracy parameter with unit roundoff Θ⁡(2−b)\Theta(2^{-b}), and the modeled format width is proportional to bb. For a concrete floating-point format, total width and significand precision must instead be distinguished: the numerical horizon uses the actual unit roundoff, not the total number of stored bits. This distinction is necessary in real mixed-precision systems:

  • •

    A softmax may compute its maximum, exponential, reduction, and division in 32-bit floating point (FP32) even when the two surrounding attention matrix products use lower precision. NVIDIA Transformer Engine, for example, documents an 8-bit floating-point (FP8) attention path with FP8 matrix multiplications and FP32 softmax (NVIDIA, 2026).

  • •

    A matrix kernel may accumulate products in a precision wider than its input and output formats. Accumulation precision therefore belongs in the arithmetic model; it does not imply that the complete attention probability tensor is stored at that precision.

  • •

    The softmax output can be cast back to a lower-precision format before the value product. Conversely, an eager implementation may retain the probability tensor for backward. These are distinct choices represented by softmax effective accuracy and bstb_{\rm st}, respectively.

  • •

    Mixed-precision training may retain full-precision master weights and optimizer state even when forward weights, activations, and gradients use a narrower format (Micikevicius et al., 2018). Such residual state is included in Memhp\operatorname{Mem}_{\rm hp}, not hidden inside an effective average bit width.

  • •

    Tiled online softmax can avoid materializing the quadratic attention matrix by saving normalization statistics and recomputing attention tiles in backward (Dao et al., 2022; NVIDIA, 2026). This changes the storage model and memory traffic, while dense attention still performs a quadratic number of score and value arithmetic operations.

These observations explain why Equations B.14 and B.15 are operation and storage ratios rather than throughput predictions. Kernel fusion, memory traffic, device-specific integer or floating-point units, communication, and parallel scheduling can make the same bit-operation count run at different wall-clock speeds. Implementations can therefore differ in speed even when these analytic counts agree.

Appendix P Extended Experimental Results

This appendix examines robustness to spectral shape and ordering, numerical formats, and pretrained-model scale, and provides detailed slope estimates and reference losses. Captions specify uncertainty for each stochastic quantity.

P.1 Candidate-Count Replication and Exponent Grid

The paired K=8K=8 versus K=32K=32 comparison in Figure 10 tests how candidate count affects the finite-sample construction and trained learner. The profile-by-budget comparison in Figure 5 tests exponent agreement. Table 4(b) gives unbinned numerical slope estimates. The two-stage study crosses four profiles and prefixes, three sample and state budgets, K=8,32K=8,32, and eight paired seeds. Each sample budget restarts the learner, whereas state budgets reuse the fitted weights. Repeated settings at the minimum n=64n=64 are aggregated within seed before bootstrapping. Display bins depend only on GμMG_{\mu_{M}}.

P.2 Routing, Interventions, and Profile Robustness

The routing measurements and learned/known/frozen comparison in Figure 3(c,f) relate retrieval quality to prediction error. The decomposition and interventions in Tables 2(c) and 2(d) isolate the error sources. Figure 6 tests allocation when the spectrum departs from an exact power law.

P.3 Stored Precision and Pretrained Transformers

At 70M and 160M, the 2-bit calibration CE reaches 114.67 and 97.78 nats, respectively. These losses exceed the pre-specified [0,20][0,20]-nat prediction range, and the fitting procedure yields no converged, in-range solutions when calibration includes 2-bit weights. At 410M–2.8B, all four response functions yield such solutions. A sensitivity analysis fits 4/8-bit and BF16 separately at every scale and predicts 6-bit loss and the largest data budget. Tables 5, 6, 7 and 8 report both calibration choices; Appendix R defines the response functions and evaluation sets.

Predicting unseen data and storage budgets.

With 4/8-bit and BF16 calibration, the additive model lowers prediction error at the largest data budget for every scale (Table 5). For 6-bit interpolation, it raises error at 70M/160M and lowers it at the four larger scales (Table 6). Each paired 95% BCa interval for these additive-minus-data differences excludes zero. An interaction further improves extrapolation at 160M, 410M and 1.4B; the corresponding intervals at the other three scales include zero. The benefit of modeling both resources therefore depends on scale and on which resource is extrapolated. Tables 7 and 8 give the predictions when calibration also includes 2-bit weights.

Appendix Q Experiment and Reproducibility Details

We retain the scientific configuration and seed- or item-level measurements for every reported result. This appendix specifies the sampling scheme, numerical formats, software environment, and aggregation procedure; the accompanying code instantiates the complete grids.

Software and execution framework.

The local central-processing-unit (CPU) runs used Python 3.11.15 with NumPy 2.0.2, SciPy 1.13.1, Pandas 2.3.3, PyArrow 21.0.0, and Matplotlib 3.9.4. The graphics-processing-unit (GPU) runs used Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.13.0 with CUDA 13.0, TorchAO 0.18.0, Transformers 5.16.1, Datasets 5.0.1, and Hugging Face Hub 1.29.0. The finitebit_exp 0.1.0 package defines the scientific grids in Python. PyTorch automatic differentiation supplies the Stage A and Stage V gradients in the mini-batch implementation. The weighted-average FP64 reference implements the same explicit scalar gradient on its theorem-specified active set. Independent worker processes run the two-stage training jobs. Pythia models are loaded once per model–format bundle and evaluated in inference mode. CPU experiments ran on an Apple M5 system; GPU experiments used an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition. Raw seed- and item-level measurements are stored in Parquet files.

Pythia items and operation count.

Tokenization is performed once per model tokenizer on the raw WikiText-103 test text, after which contiguous 2,049-token windows provide 2,048 next-token losses per item. All numerical formats receive identical item indices. The analytic operation count includes the query, key, value, and output projections; the two attention matrix products; and both feed-forward products.

Reproducible result generation.

Empirical curves are generated from seed- or item-level records using the uncertainty procedure specified in each caption.

The data–memory study crosses six energy–dimension profiles, seven model cutoffs from 16 to 1,024, and three normalized data and state budgets. It evaluates population excess CE over each finite source, including coordinates predicted with zero logit. The mini-batch two-stage study additionally uses the analytic tail proxy described in Appendix R; the fixed-source weighted-SGD study measures its omitted-coordinate loss directly. The pretrained-model comparisons use identical items for every format, including 96 paired WikiText-103 windows per model–format configuration.

Q.1 Additional coupling, robustness, and pretrained-model experiments

The additional experiments comprise a dyadic coupling test with 16 paired seeds, a two-stage study with eight paired seeds, robustness tests for three departures from exact power laws, and six Pythia sizes under six deployment formats on two datasets. The two-stage learner differentiates the Bernoulli loss through the attention-weighted network output and updates the stored value parameters; the direct finite-sample parameter construction is included as a separate likelihood-based comparator.

Six-scale weight-only post-training quantization.

All Pythia models use the fixed step143000 revision. WikiText-103 uses 96 common non-overlapping 2,048-token windows, and LAMBADA uses 512 common examples with last-token cross-entropy. The formats are bfloat16 (BF16), 8-bit integer (INT8) with one tensor scale, INT8 with one scale per output channel, 4-bit integer (INT4) round-to-nearest with groups of 128 weights, and half-quadratic quantization (HQQ) for INT4 groups of 128 or 32 weights. Every reported difference is paired with the BF16 result on the same item. Eager attention receives BF16 scores and returns FP32 softmax probabilities in the measured software stack. The evaluation microbatch is one for both datasets.

The item-level records retain model, format, dataset, item index, cross-entropy, represented weight error, quantized-parameter fraction, and output-logit divergence. Appendix P reports the detailed figures and tables.

Appendix R Joint Resource Evaluation

Fixed-source comparisons.

We vary data and value-state budgets while holding the generating distribution fixed. The same-marginal experiment samples the infinite dyadic source at χ∈{1,2}\chi\in\{1,2\}, γ=1\gamma=1, with a common normalization for both pairings. A sparse clipped Bernoulli estimator uses unbounded storage, isolating the data exponent. Unobserved coordinates contribute their actual probability mass times the zero-prediction excess cross-entropy. The seven sample budgets are 28,210,…,2202^{8},2^{10},\ldots,2^{20}; the primary slope uses the last four budgets for every seed and pairing.

The theorem’s learning algorithm.

For (χ,γ)=(0.5,0),(0.5,0.5),(1,0),(1,0.5)(\chi,\gamma)=(0.5,0),(0.5,0.5),(1,0),(1,0.5), the source contains 256 energy groups, each with dj=⌈jγ⌉d_{j}=\lceil j^{\gamma}\rceil scalar coordinates. This source size is distinct from the number of sampled regeneration blocks. We compare K=8,32K=8,32 candidates with eight independent seeds. At each n∈{28,210,…,216}n\in\{2^{8},2^{10},\ldots,2^{16}\}, we restart the projected, preconditioned SGD algorithm of Theorem C.5 from zero, using its active set, step sizes and weighted average. We implement the numerical reference in FP64. Calibration uses SA=⌈4​K​[log⁡(e​K)+n]⌉S_{A}=\lceil 4K[\log(eK)+\sqrt{n}]\rceil independent blocks. Each fitted state is encoded at BV=8,16,32,64,128,256B_{V}=8,16,32,64,128,256 bits using the theorem’s midpoint scalar format. Inactive fitted coordinates are zero before encoding; positive-width midpoint decoding also acts on those zero entries. An oracle-coordinate clipped estimator uses the same labeled blocks with the selected coordinate revealed. We report both value and routing bits, calibration and prediction samples, and the losses on 65,536 shared independent test contexts. Oracle and learned routes, before and after quantization, define signed counterfactual differences on these identical contexts.

Additional training and deployed storage.

Starting from the Pythia 70M, 160M, 410M, 1B, 1.4B, and 2.8B checkpoints at step143000, each of eight seeds follows one continued-training trajectory with checkpoints after 220,222,224,2262^{20},2^{22},2^{24},2^{26} additional WikiText-103 tokens. Training uses 2048-token contexts, an effective batch of 32,768 tokens, FP32 parameters and optimizer states, and BF16 computation. AdamW uses learning rate 10−510^{-5}, β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95), weight decay 0.1, gradient clipping at 1, and an eight-step warm-up followed by a constant learning rate. Deployment uses BF16 or group-128 symmetric 2/3/4/6/8-bit round-to-nearest linear weights. Integer payloads, scales, padding, retained BF16 parameters and metadata are all counted. Evaluation uses 96 fixed test windows and 96 fixed validation windows.

Prediction on held-out resource configurations.

We fit data-only, storage-only, additive and interacting response models on the first three training budgets at 2/4/8-bit and BF16. The 3/6-bit formats test storage interpolation, while the largest training budget tests data extrapolation. Fits use validation losses; test-window losses remain untouched until evaluation. Comparisons use paired training-seed uncertainty; the common initial pretrained checkpoint is evaluated once and its uncertainty uses windows. Let t=T/220t=T/2^{20} denote additional tokens in units of the smallest budget, and let ss be deployment-package bytes divided by the BF16 package size. Writing x=t−αx=t^{-\alpha} and y=s−β−1y=s^{-\beta}-1, the four fitted CE models are

c+a​x⏟data only,c+d​y⏟storage only,c+a​x+d​y⏟additive,c+a​x+d​y+h​x​y⏟interaction.\underbrace{c+ax}_{\text{data only}},\qquad\underbrace{c+dy}_{\text{storage only}},\qquad\underbrace{c+ax+dy}_{\text{additive}},\qquad\underbrace{c+ax+dy+hxy}_{\text{interaction}}.

We fit each model scale separately by least squares on validation CE, with c,a,d∈[0,20]c,a,d\in[0,20], α,β∈[0.01,4]\alpha,\beta\in[0.01,4], and h∈[−20,20]h\in[-20,20]. The fitting procedure requires convergence and calibration predictions in the pre-specified range [0,20][0,20] nats; held-out predictions are checked against the same range. After observing the large 2-bit losses at 70M and 160M, we also analyze 4/8-bit and BF16 calibration, with 6-bit interpolation and 4/6/8-bit/BF16 extrapolation. This sensitivity analysis uses the same response functions and parameter bounds. Root-mean-square error (RMSE) compares predicted and measured test CE across the held-out resource configurations, after averaging the 96 windows within each configuration.

Route-adjusted and complete-source losses.

Let Llr,q,Llr,u,Lor,uL_{\mathrm{lr},q},L_{\mathrm{lr},u},L_{\mathrm{or},u} denote finite-source excess CE for learned-route quantized, learned-route unquantized, and known-route unquantized predictions. All subtract the same source Bayes loss. The route-adjusted analysis defines E=Llr,q+M−χE=L_{\mathrm{lr},q}+M^{-\chi}, R+=(Llr,u−Lor,u)+R_{+}=(L_{\mathrm{lr},u}-L_{\mathrm{or},u})_{+}, and F+=(Llr,q−Llr,u)+F_{+}=(L_{\mathrm{lr},q}-L_{\mathrm{lr},u})_{+}. Its spectrum comparison uses E−R+E-R_{+}; its component sum is an upper envelope of EE. Here MM is the energy-group cutoff and M−χM^{-\chi} is an analytic tail proxy. Our fixed-source study instead evaluates the generating distribution without adding that proxy and retains all four counterfactual losses. The oracle loss splits over actual held-out targets inside and outside AnA_{n}; adding the signed differences Llr,u−Lor,uL_{\mathrm{lr},u}-L_{\mathrm{or},u} and Llr,q−Llr,uL_{\mathrm{lr},q}-L_{\mathrm{lr},u} gives exactly the complete-source excess loss Llr,qL_{\mathrm{lr},q}. The tail term is the actual zero-prediction KL on omitted targets. This identity holds per test context, before any averaging, by Proposition S.2.

Empirical and known-energy allocation.

The robustness study’s adaptive allocator uses the count-corrected score

si=[pi​θ^i2−pimax⁡{1,Ni}]+,s_{i}=\left[p_{i}\widehat{\theta}_{i}^{2}-\frac{p_{i}}{\max\{1,N_{i}\}}\right]_{+},

where NiN_{i} is the observed count and θ^i\widehat{\theta}_{i} the bounded Bernoulli maximum-likelihood estimate. Both this rule and the known-energy reference water-fill ∑isi​4−bi\sum_{i}s_{i}4^{-b_{i}}, floor widths, and assign remaining bits by marginal gains; the reference substitutes si=qis_{i}=q_{i}. The empirical subtraction prioritizes resolved coordinates, whereas the known-energy reference minimizes the true-energy distortion objective. These distinct objectives allow different finite-sample CE even at the same state budget. The unknown-exponent schedule in Theorem 5.1 is a separate, deterministic construction.

Appendix S Total Resources and Fixed-Source Evaluation

The following consequence accounts jointly for the value-learning and routing stages. Write q(r)q_{(r)} for the decreasing coordinate energies and ξ\xi for their decay exponent.

for K=1K=1, take SA=BA=0S_{A}=B_{A}=0. If deployment arithmetic has mean squared logit error at most ε/(4​CL)\varepsilon/(4C_{L}), the weighted-SGD learner has expected excess risk at most ε\varepsilon, uses N=n+SAN=n+S_{A} blocks and retains at most B=BV+BAB=B_{V}+B_{A} learned bits. N=O(ε−(1+ξ)/ξ),B=O(ε−1/ξ),SA/n→0,BA/BV→0.N=O(\varepsilon^{-(1+\xi)/\xi}),\quad B=O(\varepsilon^{-1/\xi}),\qquad S_{A}/n\to 0,\quad B_{A}/B_{V}\to 0.

For χ>0\chi>0, γ≥0\gamma\geq 0, block energies aj≍j−(1+χ)a_{j}\asymp j^{-(1+\chi)}, dimensions dj≍jγd_{j}\asymp j^{\gamma} and equal coordinate energies qj,ℓ=aj/djq_{j,\ell}=a_{j}/d_{j} within each block, the coordinate exponent is ξ=χ/(1+γ)\xi=\chi/(1+\gamma).

Proof.

shows that total width is at most (1+ξ)​m/(2​ln⁡2)≤a​m≤b(1+\xi)m/(2\ln 2)\leq am\leq b. Each retained distortion term is at most C​m−1−ξCm^{-1-\xi}, and the tail is at most (C/ξ)​m−ξ(C/\xi)m^{-\xi}. Since m≥b/(2​a)m\geq b/(2a),

Summability controls every countable tail. The theorem’s scalar implementation floors public continuous widths; this cannot exceed the bit budget and multiplies each distortion term by at most four. Its constant is already included in CLC_{L}. A public allocation needs no additional learned index code.

The ceilings in n,BVn,B_{V} can only decrease their nonincreasing error functionals, so each is at most ε/(4​CL)\varepsilon/(4C_{L}). The independent stages consume distinct blocks, totaling n+SAn+S_{A}. Each routing row is reconstructed from its count in {0,…,SA}\{0,\ldots,S_{A}\} and its destination or unseen symbol. The displayed integer-width fields encode all these possibilities. Concatenating their BAB_{A}-bit code with the value code gives at most 2BA+BV2^{B_{A}+B_{V}} retained states. Both tend to zero since ξ>0\xi>0. Adding the routing costs gives the two total-resource orders.

with separate positive c0c_{0} for the upper and lower comparisons. Inversion proves q(r)≍r−(1+χ+γ)/(1+γ)q_{(r)}\asymp r^{-(1+\chi+\gamma)/(1+\gamma)} and the asserted ξ\xi. The argument allows bounded nonmonotonicity in the original block labels. ∎

Proposition S.2 (Fixed-source loss and paired counterfactuals).

Let pp be a fixed probability distribution on a finite or countable coordinate set, |θi|≤Δi≤R|\theta_{i}|\leq\Delta_{i}\leq R, qi=pi​Δi2q_{i}=p_{i}\Delta_{i}^{2}, and d(θ,z)=DKL(Ber(σ(θ))∥Ber(σ(z)))d(\theta,z)=D_{\rm KL}(\operatorname{Ber}(\sigma(\theta))\|\operatorname{Ber}(\sigma(z))). Conditional on a fitted table |wi|≤R|w_{i}|\leq R supported on SS, a fresh oracle-routed example has excess risk

L⁡(w,oracle)\displaystyle L(w,\mathrm{oracle}) =∑i∈Spi​d​(θi,wi)+∑i∉Spi​d​(θi,0),\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in S}p_{i}d(\theta_{i},w_{i})+\sum_{i\notin S}p_{i}d(\theta_{i},0),
0≤∑i∉Spi​d​(θi,0)\displaystyle 0\leq\sum_{i\notin S}p_{i}d(\theta_{i},0) ≤18​∑i∉Sqi.\displaystyle\leq\tfrac{1}{8}\sum_{i\notin S}q_{i}.

If all |θi|=a|\theta_{i}|=a, the omitted term equals p⁡(Sc)​d​(a,0)p(S^{c})d(a,0), also for a data-dependent SS.

On the same full candidate context, let Lr​vL_{rv} be excess loss with route r∈{0,1}r\in\{0,1\} (oracle, learned) and value state v∈{0,1}v\in\{0,1\} (unquantized, quantized), with all four predicted logits in [−R,R][-R,R]. Pointwise and under every common empirical or population average,

L11\displaystyle L_{11} =L00+(L10−L00)+(L11−L10)\displaystyle=L_{00}+(L_{10}-L_{00})+(L_{11}-L_{10})
=L00+(L01−L00)+(L11−L01).\displaystyle=L_{00}+(L_{01}-L_{00})+(L_{11}-L_{01}).

The two format contrasts differ by L11−L10−L01+L00L_{11}-L_{10}-L_{01}+L_{00}; individual contrasts may be negative. If two predictions in [−R,R][-R,R] agree outside an event AA, their expected CE differs by at most 2​R​Pr⁡(A)2R\Pr(A). If AA is that some candidate lies in TT, then Pr⁡(A)≤K​p​(T)\Pr(A)\leq Kp(T).

Proof.

For target coordinate ii, conditional expected CE minus Bayes CE is exactly d⁡(θi,z)d(\theta_{i},z). Conditional on training, a fresh target retains law pp, giving ∑ipi​d​(θi,wi)\sum_{i}p_{i}d(\theta_{i},w_{i}). Nonnegative terms permit countable summation by monotone convergence. Splitting at SS, where the fitted table is zero on its complement, proves the oracle identity.

Put A⁡(z)=ln⁡(1+ez)A(z)=\ln(1+e^{z}). Direct substitution gives d⁡(θ,z)=A⁡(z)−A⁡(θ)−A′​(θ)​(z−θ)d(\theta,z)=A(z)-A(\theta)-A^{\prime}(\theta)(z-\theta). Since 0<A′′​(z)=σ⁡(z)​(1−σ⁡(z))≤1/40<A^{\prime\prime}(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\leq 1/4, Taylor’s integral remainder implies 0≤d⁡(θ,0)≤θ2/80\leq d(\theta,0)\leq\theta^{2}/8. Multiply by pip_{i}, use θi2≤Δi2\theta_{i}^{2}\leq\Delta_{i}^{2}, and sum to obtain the tail bound. Exchanging Bernoulli outcomes gives d⁡(−a,0)=d⁡(a,0)d(-a,0)=d(a,0), proving the constant-magnitude formula conditional on each fitted support.

For learned routing, ∑saQ​s​wCs\sum_{s}a_{Qs}w_{C_{s}} can be nonzero even when the target is outside SS, because a distractor may lie in SS. The four losses therefore evaluate the full context with a common target law. Cancelling intermediate terms proves both identities pointwise; linearity preserves them under averaging. Subtracting the two format contrasts gives their stated interaction. For a concrete sign example, the one-bit midpoint format on [−1,1][-1,1] sends w=0.1w=0.1 to 0.50.5. At θ=0.5\theta=0.5, the contrast is −d⁡(0.5,0.1)<0-d(0.5,0.1)<0; at θ=0.1\theta=0.1, it is d⁡(0.1,0.5)>0d(0.1,0.5)>0.

Finally, per-label CE ℓy​(z)=A⁡(z)−y​z\ell_{y}(z)=A(z)-yz has derivative σ⁡(z)−y\sigma(z)-y of absolute value at most one. Hence |ℓy​(z)−ℓy​(z′)|≤|z−z′|≤2​R|\ell_{y}(z)-\ell_{y}(z^{\prime})|\leq|z-z^{\prime}|\leq 2R. Multiplying by the indicator of AA and averaging proves the approximation bound, also after subtracting the common Bayes risk. The union bound gives Pr⁡(A)≤∑s=1KPr⁡(Cs∈T)=K​p​(T)\Pr(A)\leq\sum_{s=1}^{K}\Pr(C_{s}\in T)=Kp(T); it needs only the candidate marginals, not independence. ∎
